talks.title: Watch The Streamathon today Dec 18
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Cybersecurity Cares - Watch The Streamathon today Dec 18.
talks.summary:
Overview: Nicole from the Diana Initiative promotes the Cyber Security Cares Streamathon fundraiser supporting nonprofits that make cybersecurity healthier, more inclusive, and more sustainable.

Key Topics: Diversity barriers in information security; Diana Initiative programs including RSA and DEF CON scholar sponsorships; quiet rooms and community spaces at DEF CON; and the December fundraising campaign splitting proceeds among five nonprofits.

Technical Details: The Initiative sponsored scholars to RSA, Black Hat, and DEF CON with mentorship programs, hosted neurodivergent-friendly spaces, and supported BSides events in New York, Delaware, and Philadelphia during the prior year.

Takeaways: Cybersecurity's diversity problem requires sustained community investment. Supporting organizations like the Diana Initiative builds a healthier, more representative security workforce.

talks.title: OWASP
talks.teaser: HSC101 Hacker Summer Camp n00b analyzes OWASP.
talks.summary:
OWASP at Hacker Summer Camp

In a Hacker Summer Camp 101 interview, OWASP representative John explains the group’s Def Con outreach showing hackers and white hats share a skill spectrum. OWASP hosts hands-on trainings rather than lecture-only sessions for newcomers and veterans alike.

Hands-On Villages and Workshops

Planned activities include Juice Shop training, Hadex sessions, and ZAP plugin labs. OWASP also runs an intentionally vulnerable AI boot camp for participants who have never tried breaking ML systems. A lounge offers one-on-one help, including support for visitors in partner villages such as Blue Team Village CTFs.

Community Cross-Village Alignment

John recommends bringing a laptop for interactive workshops but warns against daily-driver devices—referencing Def Con “YOLO” burners. OWASP coordinates with Adversarial Village, Red Team Village, IC, Lonely Hackers, Diana, and WISP for cross-village learning experiences.

talks.title: Lonely Hackers Club
talks.teaser: HSC101 Hacker Summer Camp n00b details Lonely Hackers Club.
talks.summary:
Community Purpose

Star from Lonely Hackers Club (LHC) clarifies the group is not a dating site—it is a welcoming DEF CON crew for solo travelers who want friends before arriving. Originating from r/DEFCON repeat questions about hotels, parties, and badges, LHC keeps thousands registered with ~1,000 active on Telegram year-round.

Onboarding and Safety

Newcomers join via lonelyhackers.com/club Telegram, find mentors before con, and avoid first-timer panic (e.g., locating goons for badges). Host Nicole from The Diana Initiative recommends Hacker Summer Camp 101 resources, Hacker Tracker, and info booth or red-shirt goons when lost.

DEF CON Activities

LHC collaborates with OWASP, TDI, and others on resume reviews, CTFs, badge builds, workshops, and social events like group dinners (including social-engineering steakhouse outings). They occupy community space near TDI with content throughout the con, not a brief pop-up village.

Audience and Merch

Kids are generally discouraged except mature teen volunteers. LHC prioritizes community over sales, though electronic badges may appear; Telegram remains the primary engagement channel.

talks.title: Pinball High Score Contest
talks.teaser: HSC101 Hacker Summer Camp n00b examines Pinball High Score Contest.
talks.summary:
Pinball at DEF CON

Rich, a world-ranked competitive pinball player, describes how pinball became a DEF CON fixture. After years of visiting the Pinball Hall of Fame, he researched IoT-era pinball machines, found vulnerabilities that could remotely flip flippers during high-stakes tournaments, and disclosed them at ShmooCon. Stern Pinball then partnered to bring machines on-site so attendees would not have to leave the conference.

Pinball High Score Contest

Last year's contest was deliberately layered: hints appeared in forums, social media, and GitHub, and game code/settings were arranged so careful observers could hack into the finals without breaking equipment or the network. A village worker won after reporting an unfair game configuration. The event also tied into Stern Insider Connected QR badges, privacy guidance, IFPA-sanctioned play, and cross-village CTF flags embedded in games.

Advice for participants

Rich encourages newcomers to walk up and play, try unconventional paths, and ask volunteers when unsure. DEF CON contests often reward creative rule interpretation within stated boundaries.

talks.teaser: HSC101 Hacker Summer Camp n00b analyzes XR Village.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Diana Initiative's Hacker Summer Camp 101 episode introduces DEF CON's XR Village with organizer Star, covering extended-reality security and community activities.

## What XR Village Covers
"Extended reality" spans AR, VR, MR, and even persona-driven gameplay that alters perceived reality. The village hosts hardware hacking on VR headsets, social-engineering exercises, and kid-friendly challenges.

## Community Highlights
A favorite activity pairs kids with federal demo-lab operators—coaching youngsters to socially engineer serious-looking government techs into silly tasks. A 14-year-old partnered with Meta became the village's top VR hardware hacker, returning annually.

## Takeaways
XR Village blends physical device security, human manipulation skills, and inclusive outreach—visit for stickers, badge swaps, and hands-on XR threat exploration.

talks.title: Take the Stage, Take Up Space and Take The Win
talks.teaser: Offers practical guidance on conference speaking, from CFP submissions to stage presence, for security professionals building visibility.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with a visualization of delivering a successful conference talk and how that visibility can strengthen hiring, promotions, and professional reputation. It cites widespread fear of public speaking and frames stage work as a learnable craft that builds confidence, communication skills, and leadership credibility beyond security conferences alone.

The speaker ties visibility to industry diversity and knowledge sharing, arguing that varied life experience surfaces threat angles others miss. A circus aerial-silks anecdote illustrates how the simplest move often wins the crowd—and draws a parallel to straightforward attack paths such as social engineering—while stressing that no one must be expert in everything; depth in one area plus personal perspective is enough to justify a talk.

Seven practical habits close the session: rehearse until the flow is natural, stay within allotted time, favor visual slides over dense text, tailor jargon to the room, pause when flustered, apply widely to calls for papers despite rejections, and lean on mentors and peers for CFP and delivery feedback. The aim is to encourage more people to take the stage for their own goals and for the field.

talks.title: Redefining Strength: The Power of Leading
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Redefining Strength: The Power of Leading with Empathy and Embracing Vulnerability.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, cybersecurity executive and CEO Rick discusses redefining leadership strength through empathy, vulnerability, and inclusivity. Drawing on twenty years of experience in go-to-market roles across security companies such as Rapid7, Bugcrowd, Sonatype, and currently KSOC, Rick contrasts traditional command-and-control, extrovert-centric leadership styles with empathetic, human-centered approaches that foster psychological safety and team success.

### Key Topics
- **Evolution of Leadership Styles**: The shift from traditional models where vulnerability was viewed as weakness and extroversion was prioritized, toward models that accommodate diverse personalities and backgrounds.
- **Challenges Faced by Female Leaders**: Common biases and double standards in cybersecurity, including doubts about technical expertise, questions regarding co-founders, and pressure to adopt aggressive leadership demeanors.
- **The Business Case for Diversity**: Research demonstrating positive business outcomes associated with female leadership, such as stock price momentum, improved profitability, and greater gender diversity on boards.
- **Empathy in the Workplace and Culture**: Adopting core values—such as those used at Microsoft—that evaluate individuals not only on personal business impact but also on how they contribute to the success of others.
- **Supportive Company Policies**: Practical mechanisms to support employees, including generous parental leave policies for both mothers and fathers, mental health breaks, and meeting-free Fridays.

### Technical Details & Actionable Practices
Rick highlights five foundational behaviors to cultivate empathy and minimize workplace conflict:
1. **Be Present**: Disconnect from digital distractions and remain engaged during interactions.
2. **Active Listening**: Restate or summarize what others communicate to validate their perspectives and ensure they feel heard.
3. **Invest in Self-Care**: Leaders must recharge physically and mentally (e.g., exercise, taking breaks) to maintain the capacity to support others effectively.
4. **Assume Positive Intent**: Prevent workplace friction by operating under the baseline assumption that colleagues are acting in good faith rather than with malicious motives.
5. **Follow Up**: Check in regularly after discussions or difficult moments to reinforce long-term care and accountability.

### Q&A Insights and Takeaways
During the audience question-and-answer period, several leadership challenges were addressed:
- **Integrating Empathy into Onboarding**: Embedding culture into new hire orientation across departments so core values are introduced immediately.
- **Balancing Empathy with Business Performance**: Acknowledging that while leaders should not act as full-time therapists, empathetic evaluation metrics naturally curb toxic behaviors by aligning personal success with team support.
- **Scaling Company Culture and HR**: Managing HR's role as organizations expand, ensuring employee support remains genuine rather than strictly bureaucratic.
- **Setting Boundaries**: Demonstrating and respecting transparent schedule boundaries (e.g., blocking personal time, disconnecting Slack after hours) tailored to individual team needs rather than enforcing a rigid one-size-fits-all model.

talks.title: Unveiling Failures and Forging Change: Combatting Gender in Cybersecurity for Marginalized Genders
talks.teaser: Examines workforce gaps for marginalized genders in infosec and offers individual and community paths toward belonging.
talks.summary:
The session opens by framing how sex assignment, gender attribution, and daily expression shape expectations from childhood onward, then defines marginalized genders as situational rather than fixed labels. It connects that lens to cybersecurity’s stated diversity goals, arguing that belonging rarely matches policy on paper and that imposter feelings often track exclusion more than skill.

The middle draws on published workforce figures: cisgender men reportedly exceed three quarters of the field, women’s share is often quoted near one quarter but may fall near thirteen percent when roles are counted narrowly, and intersectional representation plus leadership gaps look far worse in survey data. Studies on diverse hiring slates, ally self-perception versus lived experience, pay gaps, attrition, microaggressions, and missing non-binary data illustrate why representation research itself can blind organizations.

Participants reflect in pairs on identity, stereotypes, and past misgendering before the presenter stresses self-accountability, in-room solidarity when credit is stolen, and sustained conversation despite backlash. Question time touches nonprofit fundraising for trans-inclusive work, reading room safety before debating gender, and mobilizing cisgender male allies when legal climates tighten.

talks.title: Breaking The Mold
talks.teaser: Practitioners map non-technical paths into GRC, offensive security, and architecture with mentorship and hiring guidance for diverse talent.
talks.summary:
The session frames why diverse, non-technical entrants matter in cyber, citing stagnant workforce diversity figures from a 2021 report and arguing that hiring organizations should value atypical talent and transferable skills.

Carol Vernon describes her path from social media and military intelligence into National Guard cyber exposure, an unqualified GRC hire, self-driven progression to pen testing during the pandemic, red team work, and enterprise purple teaming. She emphasizes LinkedIn visibility, offering immediate team value through public speaking and documentation work, targeted upskilling tied to employer needs, and modeling careers after respected practitioners. A planned co-presenter segment covers a six-month Aquia accelerator from zero experience to GRC and zero trust architecture at CMS/HHS, though much of that story is summarized when she arrives late.

Shared guidance covers healthy humility, owning a niche skill, competitor mindset, mentorship networks for women, evaluating paid accelerators versus predatory boot camps, learning what the current job actually uses, and defending work-life balance. The Q&A extends the theme: analytical backgrounds transfer broadly, mentors respond to specific asks, and entry-level certifications can anchor terminology.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2023-Cynthia Taylor-Human-Centered Security: Building for Accessibility in Security
talks.teaser: Explains how inaccessible security controls exclude users and open attack paths, and why accessibility belongs in early design.
talks.summary:
Cynthia Taylor frames human-centered security as an extension of human-centered design: controls built for real people, including those with permanent, temporary or situational disabilities. She separates disability, accessibility and accommodation, noting that curb cuts and text-to-speech help more people than they were built for. Her first case study is CAPTCHA, which she argues excludes blind, low-vision, deaf and dyslexic users and non-English speakers, with a more screen-reader-friendly alternative cited. A second case describes a person with vision loss who cannot complete face-based identity verification, and a WhatsApp hackathon feature that guided photo capture.

The middle of the talk treats inaccessible features as an attack surface. She reviews CVEs involving Windows and Android accessibility services, a Windows persistence technique that abuses accessibility programs launched from the login screen, and recent Android banking trojans. A 2018 spyware app that used accessibility services to read WhatsApp messages is also covered. She then turns to policy: the 2023 US National Cybersecurity Strategy on vendor liability, CISA's new strategic plan, FDA software testing requirements for medical devices, and a Justice Department proposed rule that would point public-sector websites and apps to WCAG 2.0 AA.

She closes with takeaways: an estimated 1.3 billion people have significant disabilities, and interfaces that fail them can leave a population exposed and make it an attractive target. Her advice is to bring accessibility and security into design together through shared agile conversations, rather than bolting either on or testing only at the end. The Q&A adds practical tips on colour contrast and testing with accessibility settings turned on.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2023-Kaileigh McCrea-What the Yandex Leak Tells Us About How Big Tech Uses Your
talks.teaser: Reviews leaked Yandex analytics code to show how SDKs harvest movement, Wi-Fi, and identity signals tied to ads and state telecom matching.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with the January 2023 leak of roughly 45 gigabytes of Yandex source code and the company’s public claims that AppMetrica analytics data is limited and hard to re-identify. It situates Yandex within Russian and EU political pressure, the golden share arrangement, sanctions, restructuring, and global reach of the AppMetrica SDK in hundreds of millions of apps, including VPNs.

The middle walks through leaked AppMetrica and Crypta code: hashed but still distinctive device identifiers, precise geolocation including altitude and speed, Wi-Fi SSIDs linked to Yandex IDs, demographic and household modeling, behavioral ad segments, passport and email linkage, voice biometrics from Alice smart speakers, and a matcher that exchanges fingerprinting events with major Russian telecoms including state-owned Rostelecom.

The close argues that token anonymization fails once data is glued across services, and that developers should audit third-party SDKs while users weigh long-term custody risk when ownership or government alignment changes. A brief Q&A contrasts scrutiny of Russian and Chinese firms with similar patterns elsewhere and notes limits of deletion requests versus retained analytics products.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2023-Allyn Stott-How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Build a Modern Detection
talks.teaser: Lays out a four-phase framework for modernizing detection and response, from assessing current state to reporting metrics.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who started on the red team before moving to blue team work, argues that many blue teams fail because they work ad hoc, copy what worked at a previous employer, and stay busy without a strategy. The talk contrasts a legacy detection and response program, which is reactive, tool-centric, manual and siloed, with a modern one that is proactive, business-focused, automation-first and connected to the rest of the organization.

The core of the talk is a four-phase framework adapted from organizational design: assess the current state, design and develop the ideal program, implement while handling operational challenges, and evaluate and report. Assessment covers vision, people, processes and technology, using NIST's workforce roles to build a skills heat map and CMMI to rate process maturity. Design produces a process view that tells the program's story, and an architecture view organized around capabilities rather than product categories, with MITRE ATT&CK, MITRE D3FEND and a SOC automation matrix as starting points.

For implementation, the speaker suggests temporarily outsourcing to absorb backlog and buying a solution that covers about 65 percent of needs rather than building everything. For reporting, the talk replaces raw event counts with micro purple test results showing which threats can be seen in each environment, and uses incidents as narratives across process, technology and people. An audience question on fitting stakeholder management into the framework was answered by documenting a communication contract for each stakeholder group.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2023-Tina Zhang-Powell-Managing Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure - The Art Of
talks.teaser: Shows the coordination behind two multi-vendor vulnerability disclosures and what working with vendors teaches.
talks.summary:
The talk, given by a security technical program manager at the Microsoft Security Response Center, explains coordinated vulnerability disclosure: a researcher reports a flaw, the vendor ships a fix, and only then are the details made public. It focuses on the coordination layer that sits between researchers and developers, where a team tracks many parties, deadlines and disclosure timelines at once.

The first case involved a memory allocation flaw in RTOS software used in IoT and medical devices. Researchers first reported it to a government agency in 2020, before their company was acquired by Microsoft, and the work was then routed through Microsoft's vulnerability research program. More than 31 RTOS products from 28 companies were affected, leading to 25 CVEs. The disclosure date kept moving because older products were harder to patch, and the full process took roughly eight months. The second case covered Android flaws in preinstalled carrier apps that users could not easily remove or update. Four CVEs were fixed about 60 days after reporting, but public disclosure waited four months because carriers needed forced restarts to push the updates.

The speaker's takeaways are to give vendors time to patch, keep protecting customers as the first goal, and build working relationships so that vendors see disclosure as shared work. The government agency's official vulnerability list and its authority helped keep vendors moving. The talk closed with a note that the team had grown from about 12 people when the speaker joined in 2018 to more than 30 and was still hiring.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2023-Poppaea McDermott & Jojo O'Gorman-The Virtuous Cycle of Hunt-Focused Purple
talks.teaser: Practitioners learn a repeatable purple-team cycle for OneNote abuse, from emulation through hunt hypotheses to detection rules.
talks.summary:
The speakers frame hunt-focused purple teaming as a collaborative loop: attack simulations feed threat hunting, which feeds detection engineering, then knowledge sharing closes the cycle. They argue this reduces silos between red consultants, threat hunters, and SOC teams while cutting duplicate research.

The core case study is OneNote abuse that gained traction in early 2023 as criminals moved past macro restrictions and Mark of the Web on other attachments. Using fleet-wide EDR data, they profile normal OneNote child processes and edge cases, then work with offensive consultants to run controlled executions across embedded file types and living-off-the-land binaries. Telemetry examples show file drops under temporary paths and unusual parent-child chains.

Hunting emphasizes behavioral hypotheses over brittle IOCs, baselining noisy behavior, and least-frequency analysis to spotlight rare OneNote spawning mshta, hh.exe, or wscript. They extend chains with ancestry views such as Outlook launching OneNote, cite a Qakbot-style infection, and discuss turning high-fidelity hunts into durable behavioral rules. Takeaways cover shared test data, quarterly priorities, analyst end-to-end ownership, and tuning allow lists before production deployment.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2023-Deirdre Cleary-Spilling the TEE presented
talks.teaser: Explains trusted execution environments for protecting data in use, then demos attesting an app on AWS Nitro Enclaves.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces trusted execution environments (TEEs) as a way to protect data while it is in use, the gap left after data at rest and in transit are routinely encrypted. The speaker explains the core properties a TEE should provide, namely data confidentiality, data integrity and code integrity, plus optional ones such as attestability. TEEs are grouped into hardware, cloud provider and abstraction categories, and use cases range from protecting media content and cryptographic keys to tokenization, machine learning inference and multi-party collaboration.

A central example is a period tracking app that tries to keep users' personal data out of plain text while still allowing accurate predictions and opt-in research. The speaker walks through building the app in a Docker container, deploying it to AWS Nitro Enclaves, sending a request and attesting the code. Adding a single line of logging changes the PCR0 measurement, so the attestation check fails and the speaker would not send further requests. The threat discussion covers software, protocol, cryptographic and physical attacks, along with side channels.

The closing section lists limitations: TEEs need significant engineering effort, are hard to observe, are tightly coupled to specific hardware and operating systems, and are expensive. The main takeaway is that attestation lets a user verify what is running in the enclave. The Q&A touches on adoption, which depends on maturing products and regulation, and on when a TEE suits parties who must prove security to risk-averse counterparts.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2023-Gaspard Baye-Exploring the Frontiers of Large Language Models(Generative AIs)
talks.teaser: Explains how large language models work, then walks through prompt injection, hallucination and defenses against them.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a plain introduction to AI, showing how artificial neurons imitate biological ones and how stacking them yields deep learning. It then explains large language models, covering attention, transformer architectures and the difference between base models and instruction-tuned ones, plus reinforcement learning from human feedback.

The attack section starts with a typical deployment, where user text passes through an assistant, an API and an agent before reaching the model. A public AI challenge shows prompt injection: a password the model was told to keep secret was pulled out one letter at a time. Another example injected code to read a system file, a path to remote code execution, and a third used an "ignore the above" instruction to hijack a classifier. Hallucination appears in a generated reference list where only one of three entries was real. Impacts discussed include misinformation, manipulated behaviour, privacy loss and reputational harm.

Defenses discussed include models trained to refuse harmful requests, but the speaker stresses that user input should always be sanitized rather than trusted. Hallucination mitigations such as changed decoding and grounding answers in external sources were presented, though no method was called fully reliable. For practitioners, vendor-hosted models shift much of the security burden to the provider, while in-house or open-source models need internal review and vetted training data. The talk ends with responsible AI principles: bias mitigation, transparency, accountability, privacy and fairness.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2023-KillrBunn3-Mischievous Goots: Atomic Testing and Gootloader
talks.teaser: Walks through a Security Onion lab and Atomic Red Team tests that mimic Gootloader, to check whether detections actually fire.
talks.summary:
The talk addresses a practical question: how do you know whether your detections catch a real threat? The presenter, a managed detection and response analyst, builds a small isolated lab in VirtualBox. A pfSense firewall guards an internal network that holds a Windows test machine and a Security Onion sensor. The Windows host forwards event logs through a Winlogbeat agent, and the sensor also watches network traffic. Setup steps that often cause trouble get particular attention, including the Winlogbeat configuration and adding the agent to the Defender exclusion list.

With the lab running, the talk turns to Atomic Red Team, a free, open-source library of simulated attack techniques. The presenter wrote tests based on Gootloader, a malware family that uses search engine poisoning to lure victims into downloading a zip file containing obfuscated JavaScript. The tests reproduce its behaviour: running JavaScript through wscript, collecting system and environment data, base64 encoding it, sending it out in HTTP cookies, and creating a scheduled task for persistence. The presenter then searches Security Onion alerts, the hunt view and Kibana logs for each test. A test with no alert is presented as a blind spot in detection coverage, and the talk stresses hunting from a worst-case compromise backward.

The final section connects the lab to production work. New detections should be tested in staging, tuned to reduce false positives, and then re-checked on a schedule with automated atomic tests so that changes in the environment do not break them. Practitioners take away a repeatable way to validate detections, a method for building and hunting through logs, and community rule sets and playbooks they can load into their own environments.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2023-George Sandford-Don’t Get Tangled Up in Your Cape: Hero Culture as a Negative
talks.teaser: Outlines how security hero culture drives burnout, gatekeeping, and silos and prescribes team recognition, boundaries, and help norms.
talks.summary:
George opens by distinguishing true heroism from “hero culture” in information security: marketing, reward programs, and internal language that cast analysts as invulnerable solo saviors. He ties that mindset to familiar workplace signs—constant firefighting, weekend saves, and rock-star recognition—and argues culture shapes daily behavior more than strategy.

The middle of the talk traces how heroes need villains, often casting users as adversaries and deepening us-versus-them silos. That separation erodes adoption of security practices, hoards knowledge, and rewards last-minute rescues over boring fundamentals such as documentation and network segmentation. He illustrates gatekeeping through unrealistic intern interview questions, tricks like “what happens when you Google,” and pressure to endure toxic employers as rites of passage. Homophily and tolerating “brilliant jerks” further break teams; hero norms also normalize sleep deprivation, overwork, and harmful community behavior, with burnout and turnover as outcomes. He cites workforce shortage figures in the roughly 2.5 to 3.5 million unfilled roles range and mental-health research from the community.

He closes with change levers: inclusive hiring and job descriptions, team-based recognition instead of hero awards, bystander intervention, codes of conduct, modeling healthy boundaries, and making it acceptable to ask for help—including his “ok2 ask for help” initiative. Q&A touches on teams slowly shifting toxic cultures and prioritizing mental health over any single job.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2023-Tanya Janca-Keynote Shifting Security Everywhere
talks.teaser: Argues security must cover the full development lifecycle and live apps, with practical steps for working alongside developers.
talks.summary:
Tanya Janca argues that moving security earlier in development, often called shifting left, is not enough. She describes a broader approach to application security that covers new software across the whole software development life cycle and also the applications already running in production. Her point is that older deployed apps are often the ones attackers target, so they need attention too.

For the build phase she recommends lightweight documentation: short security requirements, concise secure coding guidance, a consistent design review format rather than long questionnaires, and informal one-hour threat models. She stresses that tools only work when teams are shown how to use them, that security tasks must be scheduled into project plans, and that automated scans belong in the pipeline only where they do not frustrate developers. Security champions embedded in each team, backed by leadership support, help the program scale.

For systems already live, she covers building an inventory of apps and APIs, running a quick scan across everything for triage, logging and monitoring to detect incidents sooner, agreed fix deadlines, and metrics that show whether things are improving. She also argues that security should be presented to the business as help rather than a blocker: explain dashboards instead of sending raw numbers, tell stakeholders about upcoming projects, recognise developers' fixes, and review postmortems regularly.

talks.title: Wondering what is in the 2023 electronic badge kit? here is a preview!
talks.teaser: A component-by-component preview of the 2023 electronic badge kit, covering PCBs, a Pico H, LEDs, resistors, and AAA battery power.
talks.summary:
The segment opens as a hands-on inventory of everything shipped in the 2023 electronic badge kit. The presenter starts with two custom printed circuit boards and a Raspberry Pi Pico H that already has headers soldered on, noting that a later segment will cover flashing the board for MicroPython and running the script that turns the build into digital dice.

Most of the walkthrough is a parts tour with brief roles for each item. A 4017 Johnson decade counter receives a signal from the Pico and steps LEDs on the smaller add-on board. A switch decides whether the Pico runs from battery power. A 2×3 pin header joins the add-on to the main badge. The kit includes twenty-five 3 mm red LEDs—fourteen for the badge, ten for the add-on, and one spare—plus fifteen 1206 100 Ω resistors and a 147 Ω resistor for the add-on. Assembly helpers include a double-sided foam sticker for the holder and a three-AAA battery holder; additional holders are expected at the makers village.

Practitioners treating conference badges as teaching hardware get a clear bill of materials before soldering or firmware work. Knowing which LED count, resistor values, and interconnect header belong to the main badge versus the add-on makes troubleshooting and pre-event prep easier, even though flashing and the dice demo belong to follow-on material.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2022-Miki Demeter-Closing Keynote
talks.teaser: A closing keynote maps decades of industry pivots to practical rules for showing initiative without career-limiting missteps.
talks.summary:
The closing keynote opens by situating the Diana Initiative as a diversity-focused security conference and connecting it to earlier talks on inclusion and professional networking. The speaker then recounts a long personal path from automotive repair through medical cable manufacturing, telecom and conferencing software, to product security work at a major chipmaker, including an early lesson where unsanctioned machine maintenance ruined large production runs.

Midway, the talk turns from biography to career philosophy. Initiative that helps at home or in chores does not always translate to the workplace. The speaker describes three maturing attitudes toward being right, cites research on the proactive paradox—where unsanctioned helpfulness can hurt managers and budgets—and contrasts reckless solo action with assessing, strategizing, teaming, and asking clarifying questions before acting.

The close reframes “take the initiative” as assess, strategize, then proceed with team-aware judgment rather than heroics. Community roles in Portland tech groups, women-in-tech education, and local public service illustrate giving back. The session ends with interactive giveaways tied to conference memorabilia and a thank-you to attendees.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2022-Guy Barnhart-Magen and Brenton Morris-The Log4J Rollercoaster - from an ...
talks.teaser: An incident response team recounts Log4j discovery, coin-miner cases, and a local callback-based scanner released to the community.
talks.summary:
Two incident responders from a cyber crisis management firm frame Apache Log4j as an exhausting week-long ride that began with social-media chatter about a Minecraft-related flaw and quickly turned into widespread panic. Within roughly a day of public exploit code appearing, they tied coin-miner activity on a client network to the same attack strings others were discussing online, then faced a harder problem: customers could not tell which appliances and dependencies actually ran the library without software bills of materials, trustworthy vendor advisories, or runtime visibility.

They rejected early community scanners that proved vulnerability through DNS callbacks to third-party infrastructure, then built a local network tool that probed responsive hosts and used a fake LDAP listener so only genuinely vulnerable systems would call back. Iterations shipped across the first days of the crisis; the team used it at scale across large address spaces, documented vendor denials contradicted by proof-of-exploitation, and open-sourced the scanner while contributing to community appliance lists. The speakers also describe maintainer backlash during the holiday season and a donation attempt that highlighted how little upstream support the widely embedded project had received.

For defenders, they argue that emergent CVEs like this are still incident-response problems even without an active intruder: lean on existing EDR, memory and process hunts, log correlation for exploit strings, pre-built escalation paths, durable logging, and accurate asset records. Reusable command-line tooling, parallel scanning, and an IR mindset can shorten time to answer the central question—whether Log4j is present and exploitable—before mining malware and follow-on abuse arrive.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2022-Jessie Richardson and Heidi Winter-The Kids Are All Right
talks.teaser: Presenters describe delivering children's cybersecurity workshops in Papua New Guinea and publishing reusable event frameworks.
talks.summary:
The session opens with Kids Security Day, an Australian volunteer effort that began in 2017 to offer hands-on security and STEM workshops for young people when few comparable programs existed locally. The speakers trace growth from early events modeled on youth capture-the-flag experiences through nationwide workshops, online delivery during lockdowns, and partnerships such as indigenous cyber games.

The core case study covers a week-long pilot in Papua New Guinea with the CPL Foundation, where digital literacy and infrastructure were limited. The team ran junior, senior, and train-the-trainer sessions using workshops on coding, physical lock ethics, online footprints, cyber safety, team drone challenges, and a CTF day built on CTFd. They adapted language and exercises when local flyers signaled lower baselines, avoided awkward keyboard symbols, validated lessons on day two, and used dashboards to spot struggling participants while mentoring individuals.

The closing section presents a five-part framework—people, policies, platforms, education, and events—covering mentor vetting, consent, platform privacy, age and skill grouping, 45-minute sessions, and continuous feedback. Practitioners gain a concrete model for ethical youth outreach, low-tech accommodations, and sustained local delivery after trainers return home, plus openly shared planning materials others can tailor.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2022-Jasmine Henry-372 Million Data Points and a Few Strong Opinions on the State
talks.teaser: Shares graph-based research on enterprise cyber assets, cloud finding backlogs, and attack path metrics for risk prioritization.
talks.summary:
The presentation walks through quantitative research drawn from roughly 1,270 opted-in organizations, spanning 372 million data points modeled as a knowledge graph of cyber assets, attributes, findings, and policies. It contrasts today’s scale—on the order of 165,000 assets per organization and a finding backlog averaging 120,561 unresolved items—with older IT eras, and argues that cloud-driven scanner noise, findings averaging 383 days old, and roughly nine cloud hosts per physical device leave teams overwhelmed and poorly served by list-oriented workflows.

Key threads include the dominance of cloud assets and cloud security findings, policy-as-code sprawl versus asset growth, dependence on third-party code (over 91% of application code), and the need for automation-first remediation and honest leadership conversations about supply-chain exposure. The speaker previews ongoing “attack surfaces and paths” work on a larger dataset, citing John Lambert’s attackers-think-in-graphs idea, internet distance distributions for assets, and comparisons showing older enterprises often have longer attack paths while critical hosts and code stores show shorter, more predictable paths.

Practitioners are urged to treat automated asset inventory as mandatory, prioritize by relationship and blast radius rather than raw finding counts, and experiment with local versus global risk exposure along paths—using graph connectivity measures such as PageRank—to decide where controls matter most.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2022-Sue Spencer-Using S.M.A.R.T. Feedback to fight inappropriate communication ...
talks.teaser: A practical framework helps professionals judge workplace feedback and demand specific, respectful, actionable guidance.
talks.summary:
Workplace reviews, stand-ups, and hallway comments often deliver vague hostility or personality judgments instead of guidance that helps someone improve. The speaker presents a SMART feedback lens—specific, measurable, actionable, achievable, realistic, relevant, and respectful—arguing that effective feedback must produce dated action items, resources, and success measures rather than feelings or generic goals like “just improve.”

The talk contrasts professional evaluation with patterns to reject: “we think” without data, gossip without direct quotes, comparisons to other employees, military-style anecdotes, and rushed “drive-by” criticism. A call-center rollout example shows how blaming one agent for customer complaints ignores thin training before go-live and missing reference material; the speaker asks for percentages, team baselines, and training schedules instead. Agile stand-ups should stay respectful and focused; interrupting and rambling undermine the team even when one person performs well.

Listeners can use the model to push back calmly—request quotes, timelines, training dates, and partial credit on progress—and to give better feedback as managers without shaming. A Q&A extends the framework to feelings-based criticism, peer interruptions, frustration lists in stand-ups, and scheduling follow-ups when colleagues stall with endless questions.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2022-Ruchira Pokhriyal-The Real Cost of Free: What you need to know before ...
talks.teaser: Shows how free apps pay their way through user data, trackers and permissions, and what users can do about it.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the question of what a free app really costs its users. It explains that free app developers usually earn money through advertising, in-app purchases, paid add-ons and embedded trackers, and that the personal data collected along the way is often sold or shared. Examples of personally identifiable information, such as names, identifiers, contact details and device addresses, show how much can be learned about a person.

The middle section reviews a 2018 analysis of popular free apps on the Google Play Store and Apple App Store. Email addresses were the most requested personal detail, and camera, location, microphone and text-message permissions were flagged as risky. The speaker separates selling data from sharing it through partnerships, then covers location-based advertising, an app that exposed Wi-Fi access point details, and several GDPR fines against companies that mishandled personal data. Malicious free apps, trojans, overlays and spyware are described as direct threats.

The closing advice is practical: question every permission an app asks for, avoid signing in through social media, decline bundled toolbars, install only from official stores, read privacy policies, keep apps updated and delete unused ones. The takeaway is that free apps are paid for somehow, and users should decide whether that exchange is acceptable.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2022-Rose Songer-GRC - The Swiss Army Knife
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Diana Initiative 2022-Rose Songer-GRC - The Swiss Army Knife.
talks.summary: Rose Songer reframes governance, risk, and compliance as an organizational Swiss army knife rather than a blocking function. She outlines the governance, risk, and compliance pillars, common failure modes such as checkbox audits, manual vendor reviews, and misaligned leadership buy-in, then maps relationships across legal, sales, engineering, and customer teams. Her pronged approach stresses upward, sideways, and downward communication tuned to company culture, advocacy that embeds security into business roadmaps, cross-training on controls, metrics that prove operational maturity, and automation for vendor and access reviews. Takeaways urge vulnerable relationship building, simplicity over sprawling processes, correct communication channels, and earlier integration with sales questionnaires to protect revenue timelines.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2022-Shruthi Kamath-Connecting Dots Between Security Teams & Customer Expectations
talks.teaser: Shares project management tips for security consultants who must turn unclear client requests into delivered results.
talks.summary:
The talk examines the gap that often opens between what a customer asks a security team for and what the team delivers. Requests can be vague or misunderstood: a client asking for a penetration test may actually need compliance evidence or data protection, so asking why matters.

Several practices follow. Empathy means working with clients as partners, illustrated by a cloud testing engagement where a newcomer to penetration testing was guided at each step and later described the team as partners. Going above and beyond is shown through two clients with many applications to test, where the team planned the whole project and sent regular updates. Regular communication means flagging a likely report delay early so the customer can plan around it. Direct honesty means saying plainly when a timeline or requirement cannot be met, which the speaker says clients have appreciated.

The talk closes with constant check-ins and feedback, such as asking for a net promoter score to learn what works, and following up with dissatisfied clients to find out how to win them back. Silence from a client should not be read as satisfaction. The main takeaways are to ask why, to act as a partner focused on solving problems, and to keep empathy at the centre of the work, since it is not only about the technology.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2022-Breanne Boland-How to Become a Security Partner (and Why You Should)
talks.teaser: Explains what a security partner role involves day to day, what employers ask for, and whether the job suits you.
talks.summary:
Breanne Boland, who works as a security partner on a product security team, explains that the role acts like an internal consultant. Day to day, the work covers feature reviews, security education such as onboarding and training, writing documentation for recurring problems, helping shape security policy, and watching internal chat and roadmaps to step in early. She separates scalable work, like docs and training, from relationship work that cannot be automated, such as one-to-one conversations with product managers and engineers.

She compares the role with developer advocacy, since both jobs share a need for broad technical experience and strong writing and speaking skills, but advocates answer outside users while security partners answer internal teams. She then reviews job postings from several companies. Recurring requirements include threat modeling experience, the ability to relate risk to business leaders, comfort with ambiguity, and persistence. Postings vary in seniority, focus area and certifications, and specific requirements can leave room for candidates who lack some of them.

To close, she lists perks such as varied days, frequent context switching and friendships across engineering. Downsides include heavy meeting loads, little feature shipping, and explaining the same issues to new audiences. People can enter the role from software engineering, application security or simply being the technical person others ask. Her advice is to practise explaining technical topics to non-technical listeners and to gain hands-on experience with how software is built and deployed.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2022-Michelle Brenner-Being Your Own Project Manager
talks.teaser: Outlines stakeholder voting, quarterly reviews, and low-overhead planning engineers use without a dedicated project manager.
talks.summary:
Michelle Brenner, a senior software engineer, frames project management as a skill every engineer needs as assignments become less prescriptive. She describes teams that feel busy yet show little outward progress, and argues for building consensus on the actual problem before debating solutions, using short trials rather than permanent mandates imposed from above.

Her workflow favors low-overhead tools while processes are still changing, migration steps that pause in-flight work cleanly, and an impact–effort matrix to separate quick wins from thankless time sinks. She maps stakeholders at management, partner-team, and user levels, sets expectations about tradeoffs, and uses a simple voting exercise where each stakeholder group gets three votes on a written project list. Ongoing habits emphasize transparent work, predictable velocity, and quarterly reviews that celebrate output, check whether priorities still fit, and surface accomplishments to leadership through success statements tied to measurable outcomes.

She closes by documenting recurring steps in a living SOP, automating what repeats, and training others to lead reviews so the system does not collapse when she moves on. Audience questions touch on coaching individuals to write their own success stories and engaging engineers who usually defer to dedicated project managers.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2022-Karishma Asthana-"Hacking" Your Career: How to Successfully Pivot to your ...
talks.teaser: Uses the hacker methodology as a framework for planning a career pivot from penetration testing into product marketing.
talks.summary:
The talk applies the hacker methodology of reconnaissance, exploitation, post-exploitation and privilege escalation as a lens for changing career direction, especially for people moving into security from another field or shifting between security roles. The speaker, a product marketing manager who previously worked as a penetration tester, explains why pivots matter in a field that needs generalists as well as specialists. Her own path began with a software engineering internship and a senior-year push toward full-time engineering roles that did not suit her.

For her reconnaissance stage she took stock of personal traits, using personality tests and word banks to find language that described who she was. That pointed her toward consulting and then a penetration testing role at a large consulting firm. When she applied for product roles, her resume still emphasised tools and vulnerability counts, so she reframed her experience in business terms: persuading developers to fix code, training testers from mixed backgrounds, and finding information efficiently. Presented that way, she landed a first product marketing role at a security company.

For the audience she maps the same stages onto their own careers. The steps include listing strengths and weaknesses, considering how they act outside work, using informational interviews to ask about traits rather than a single route, and closing gaps by building skills in the target field, such as starting a blog. She also notes that some hiring managers look for software developers to bring new perspectives. The talk closes by arguing that generalists add value and that broader careers can strengthen the industry.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2022-Jackie Bow-Take a Deep Breadth
talks.teaser: Attendees gain a framework for security careers emphasizing breadth, foundational skills, and purpose over rigid specialization.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by naming the anxiety of chasing one perfect career path in security, where depth and hyper-specialization are treated as the only legitimate route. She links that mindset to gatekeeping, homogeneous hiring expectations, and the scale of open roles, and argues that curiosity across attackers, defenders, builders, and responders fits the field better than a single narrow identity.

Drawing on moves through malware analysis, incident response, threat detection, cloud and product security, engineering management, and director-level program design, she treats sideways or painful job changes as compounding experience rather than mistakes. She shares guidance on foundational learning (how you learn, first principles in systems and networks, security history, human behavior), separating self-worth from job titles, and finding a personal motivating purpose that may diverge from early technical ambitions.

She closes by encouraging listeners to ignore rigid critics, iterate on industry norms from within, and help widen who belongs in security—showing up authentically as part of reshaping the ecosystem toward sustainable, diverse careers.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2022-Christina Stokes-AIs: ATS & Your Cybersecurity Job Search
talks.teaser: Shows job seekers how applicant tracking systems filter resumes and how to align skills and keywords to get noticed.
talks.summary:
The talk is aimed at people moving into cybersecurity, whether from another field or from within IT. The speaker outlines the main cybersecurity domains, including governance and compliance, threat intelligence, offensive and defensive work, and cloud security, and suggests asking which of them fit your interests and goals. She then covers transferable skills such as problem solving, analytical reasoning and writing, and recommends volunteering and professional groups as ways in.

The middle section explains applicant tracking systems. Hiring teams use them to filter large applicant pools by matching job-description keywords, often through linked portals such as LinkedIn. Their language processing is limited, so formatting and wording can cause a qualified resume to be rejected. The speaker advises mirroring the wording of each job posting, using simple fonts and standard file formats, avoiding acronyms a parser may miss, and checking a resume against a match-scoring tool before applying.

The talk closes on ethics. Keyword stuffing and hidden white text are presented as unethical, since recruiters can spot them and the resume will be rejected. Resumes should stay truthful and be tailored to each role. The practical takeaway is to build a separate resume and cover letter for each posting, aligned to that job's own language.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2022-Kaileigh McCrea-You're Gonna Need A Bigger Boat: Building Technical Solutions
talks.teaser: Explores how privacy engineers design compliance tooling when evolving laws, ad tech, and user harm collide.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with a software bug that merged sensitive account data across users, including a case that put a domestic violence survivor at greater risk, and uses that to frame why technical choices in privacy and security carry stakes comparable to physical safety. The speaker argues that engineers across specialties now face GDPR, CCPA, fintech, and health rules without training, and describes building a privacy compliance product in ad tech that maps tracking and consent on publisher pages.

The middle walks through operational themes she labels predicament, attribution difficulty, and gray zones where behavior feels wrong but may not be clearly illegal. She details a consent-mismatch process for the IAB Transparency and Consent Framework: user-story thinking, control flows, edge cases, and client-side blocking with tension between false negatives costing revenue and false positives creating liability. Examples include an ad tech vendor shipping a hard-coded accept-all consent string, invasive browser fingerprinting justified as anti-fraud, and widespread dark-pattern cookie banners that hide enabled tracking behind a seemingly safe save action.

Closing guidance urges end-to-end ethical review in engineering workflows, early engagement with legal and compliance during design, advocating for end users, and reasoning from what consumers would reasonably expect. She recommends a trusted sounding board with diverse viewpoints rather than carrying these judgments alone.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2022-Gabrielle Botbol-Android Application Hacking
talks.teaser: Walks through an Android app pentest from lab setup and manifest review to Burp traffic analysis and reporting.
talks.summary:
The talk is an introduction to Android application penetration testing from an offensive security consultant. It walks through the usual pentest phases for a mobile app: agreeing scope and legal terms with the client, reconnaissance, static analysis, dynamic analysis and reporting. Because the lab matters more here than in other pentests, the speaker sets up an Android emulator with ADB, Jadx for decompiling code, and Burp Suite as an intercepting proxy, including installing the Burp certificate on the device.

Static analysis starts with the Android manifest, checking backup and debuggable flags, minimum SDK, requested permissions and exported activities. A social media app is used as an example of permissions that seem out of place. Resource strings are then searched for hardcoded API keys, Firebase endpoints with weak configuration, comments holding credentials, and cloud keys. In dynamic analysis, traffic is intercepted in Burp, and one case shows a sensitive banking-style screen still visible after the app is sent to the background. The practice apps PIVAA and InjuredAndroid are used throughout.

Automated tools such as MobSF and Qark can speed up the work, but the speaker stresses that findings must be verified manually because scanners produce false positives. The report structure is explained: an executive summary for management, then technical findings with a CVSS score, context, remediation and evidence, with screenshots stripped of sensitive data before sending. The key takeaway is to obtain authorization from the app owner before any testing.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2022-Ayan Islam-Breaking Silos: Your Operational Experience Is Needed in Legisla...
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Diana Initiative 2022-Ayan Islam-Breaking Silos: Your Operational Experience Is Needed in Legisla....
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk presented at Diana Initiative 2022, Ayan Islam—Associate Policy Director of Cybersecurity and Emerging Threats at the R Street Institute and former IT specialist at CISA—addresses the significant divide between frontline cybersecurity practitioners and policymakers. Islam argues that while there is an enormous workforce deficit in cybersecurity broadly, an even sharper deficit exists in legislative and policy bodies. Practitioners with operational, hands-on experience are desperately needed to inform policymaking to ensure laws, regulations, and executive actions are technically sound and operationally feasible.

### Key Topics
- **Legislative Knowledge Deficit:** As of 2015, only seven out of 3,500 legislative staff had formal technology training. While programs like Tech Congress helped raise this number above 65, Congress faces an influx of proposed legislation—over 498 cybersecurity-related proposals in the current session alone, with nine passing into law.
- **Operational Consequences of Policy:** Disconnects frequently arise between high-level policy mandates and frontline implementation. As an example, the Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act (CIRCIA) of 2021 mandates ransomware incident and data breach reporting for critical infrastructure entities to CISA within specific timeframes. Security Operations Centers (SOCs) face practical hurdles aggregating, triaging, and automating logs to meet these compliance demands without breaking ongoing operations.
- **Pathways for Engagement:** Practitioners can bridge the silo through several structured avenues:
  - *Fellowships:* Programs such as Tech Congress, CISA’s Innovation Fellows program, and the Google Public Policy Fellowship.
  - *Community & Advocacy Initiatives:* Efforts like Share the Mic in Cyber to elevate underrepresented practitioners, particularly Black cybersecurity professionals.
  - *Grassroots & Industry Groups:* I Am The Cavalry, sector-specific Information Sharing and Analysis Centers (ISACs) such as Aviation ISAC and Financial Services ISAC, and localized efforts like the Michigan Cyber Civilian Corps or local BSides events.
  - *Public Writing and Commenting:* Submitting public comments on proposed rules, publishing blog posts, and authoring op-eds.

### Technical Details & Implementation Context
Islam highlights that policy decisions directly dictate technical priorities. For instance, incident reporting rules require organizations to build automated logging pipelines and incident response triage workflows capable of producing regulatory disclosures rapidly. When technical practitioners participate early—such as redlining draft bills, participating in ISAC working groups, or commenting during agency rulemaking—they help prevent regulations that create unintended operational disruption in areas like Industrial Control Systems (ICS) and SCADA environments.

### Takeaways
- Cyber practitioners must view their operational experience as valuable input for public policy.
- Companies should consider investing in in-house cyber policy teams that actively collaborate with software developers, engineers, and subject matter experts.
- Engaging directly—via fellowship leaves of absence, industry working groups, grassroots bodies, or formal public comments—ensures that technical realities shape future cyber legislation.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2022-Lea Snyder-Hacking your way to better outcomes through negotiations
talks.teaser: Negotiation frameworks cover myths, BATNA, anchoring, offer prep, and partnering with dev teams when security fixes stall.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by framing negotiations as a learnable skill security professionals need for job offers and daily work, not an innate talent or a mandatory fight. She walks through common myths: negotiating is not always required or risk-free, not everything is negotiable at large employers, and practice beats the idea that great negotiators are born. Core vocabulary includes BATNA (best alternative to a negotiated agreement) and anchning, with warnings about unreasonable anchors and self-reported compensation outliers.

Most of the session focuses on offer negotiations: brief rapport with recruiters, gathering range and bonus or equity flexibility, never accepting immediately, researching pay through networks and sites while discarding single outlier data points, deciding priorities, articulating rationale, and making deliberate concessions. She shares personal outcomes such as a large total-comp increase after market conversations, plus cautionary tales where offers were rescinded after context-free demands. Tabletop practice with supportive and adversarial partners is emphasized before live calls.

The close applies the same mindset at work, using a vague vulnerability-versus-feature-release scenario to research product importance, dev-team culture, compensating controls, and partnership language before escalation. Further resources include prior Diana Initiative salary talks, Getting to Yes, MOOCs, and levels.fyi. Practitioners should leave with structured prep habits, calmer tactics, and ways to advocate without assuming the other side is aligned.

talks.title: point training for volunters 2022
talks.teaser: A walkthrough shows volunteers how to create a Point account, claim conference shifts, and change or cancel assignments.
talks.summary:
A volunteer coordinator for the Diana Initiative explains how in-person and remote helpers register through the Point volunteer system ahead of the conference. The session opens on the event listing URL, where shifts appear by day and time with short role descriptions, and walks through choosing a slot such as staff registration.

The demo covers creating a Point account with email verification, completing the profile including required fields and cause selections, then confirming a shift signup. The speaker notes that volunteers should avoid double-booking overlapping shifts. After logout, sign-in at pointapp.org exposes the profile and Diana Initiative event, where upcoming assignments can be changed or canceled and alternate roles selected when a slot is full.

Practitioners staffing community conferences get a concrete operational picture: which screens to expect, that profile data can be minimal or placeholder where allowed, and that shift changes run through the volunteer area until confirmed. Questions are directed to the coordinator on Discord.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2022-Sivaranjani Sankaralingam-How I hacked into the OFO Bikes in Singapore
talks.teaser: Demonstrates replaying captured GATT writes to take control of yellow shared bicycles over Bluetooth Low Energy.
talks.summary:
The presentation walks through security research on ofo’s yellow dockless bikes in Singapore around 2018, when the service was widely used via a mobile app that unlocked bicycles over Bluetooth Low Energy rather than classic Bluetooth. The speaker frames the work as personal experience from a university-linked startup setting, notes responsible disclosure with the vendor, and reminds the audience the company later ceased operating in Singapore.

After outlining GATT services and characteristics, exclusive BLE connections, pairing stages, and the difference between Just Works, six-digit passkey, and out-of-band pairing, the talk describes security modes and levels on the devices. The attack chain uses a BLE sniffer, Wireshark, and tooling such as a Bluefruit module and Nordic’s Connect app to sit between the legitimate app and a bike. Observed traffic includes three write sequences; one bike response carries a constant per-bike identifier beginning with fixed patterns, and the final command stays the same across tests—conditions that make replay straightforward. Replaying the captured writes unlocks a locked bike and can lock one already in use.

Closing guidance urges maximum feasible pairing security (including out-of-band where possible), dynamic rather than static protocol values, Android app obfuscation, server-side detection of abnormal lock cycles per user profile, and hardening inputs plus on-device and backend communication paths against relay and man-in-the-middle abuse.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2022-Dr. Mahasin Midgette-Authentic Inclusion and Building Cultures that go Beyond
talks.teaser: Shows managers how servant leadership and diversity frameworks can push organizations toward authentic inclusion.
talks.summary:
The talk examines why many organizations stall after diversity efforts and fail to become authentically inclusive. The speaker ties this gap to implicit racial and gender bias and to costs such as turnover, lost talent, lower productivity and toxic workplaces. Inclusion is presented as the condition that lets a diverse workforce function, with leadership shaping the culture.

Three conceptual frameworks are introduced. Servant leadership, drawing on Robert Greenleaf, comes first because leaders who put people first build the psychological safety that makes change possible. An organizational culture model with three levels (artifacts, espoused values and basic assumptions) shows how daily leader behavior shapes culture. A diversity management framework combines institutional and resource theory, and the speaker argues that all three should feed one combined framework.

For practical steps, the speaker recommends a leadership team anchored by a servant leader and a written diversity and inclusion framework aligned with business objectives. Training should be ongoing rather than a single annual course, supported by a diversity training task force and manager training. Pilot programs run in phases, with outcomes measured through whether employees feel valued and whether policies succeed. The takeaway is that inclusion requires sustained commitment rather than one-off policy statements.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2022-Aarti Gadhia and Sherifat Akinwonmi-Don’t settle for less - know your value!
talks.teaser: Practical guidance on researching pay, negotiating offers, and closing compensation gaps for underrepresented security professionals.
talks.summary:
The session opens with a staged job-offer scenario and audience poll showing that most people do not negotiate, then frames why that matters amid inflation and persistent pay gaps for women, women of color, and other underrepresented groups. The presenters share personal career paths in cybersecurity and outline four common blockers: fear of rejection, impostor syndrome, assumptions that you must prove yourself first, and simply not knowing market rates.

They structure practical advice around why self-worth matters, who owns closing a gap, when to negotiate or walk away, and where to research compensation. Examples include compounded lifetime earnings from a modest initial increase, asking recruiters for budget ranges instead of disclosing current pay, scoring multiple offers on culture and flexibility, and using mentors, Glassdoor, and professional networks when public data is scarce.

Closing tips emphasize making a prepared ask, pausing before accepting, practicing negotiation conversations, knowing when to stop, and negotiating beyond base salary through vacation, hybrid work, benefits, bonuses, and equity. Hiring managers are urged to advocate for fair team pay and transparency, while candidates are encouraged to align offers with personal values and refuse roles that show cultural red flags.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2022-Elle Stehli-Crossing the Finish Line - How to Train for and Achieve Your Goals
talks.teaser: Maps marathon-style training onto steady study plans, support networks, and low-cost resources for newcomers entering security.
talks.summary:
The speaker frames breaking into security like distance running: pick a finish line, train with a plan, and keep moving even when progress feels slow. Early sections address overwhelm at first conferences, imposter feelings, and the lack of a single canonical career path, then walk through assessing current skills, interests across offensive, defensive, and specialty domains, and real constraints such as weekly hours, deadlines, money, and scholarships.

Practical planning covers SMART goals, certifications, labs, courses, job-hunting benchmarks, and opinions on boot camps versus free material. The middle emphasizes starting despite imperfect conditions—libraries, phones, spare hardware, Linux, and public federal training—and building supporters online or at local events while screening unhelpful criticism from people without relevant experience.

Later guidance covers rest days, avoiding burnout, fun side activities like local BSides, capture-the-flag events, lock picking, and badges, pushing through motivation crashes near the end, celebrating wins, and reflecting before setting the next goal. The closing message is that anyone engaging with the field already belongs in security, regardless of job title or pace compared with others.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2022-Elaine Harrison-Neukirch-Kicking Imposter Syndrome to the Curb
talks.teaser: A session reframes imposter self-doubt, urges leaving toxic jobs, and peer mentor circles to rebuild security career confidence.
talks.summary:
The session opens by reframing imposter syndrome away from “fraud” toward persistent self-doubt, perfectionism, overwork, and fear of speaking up in meetings. The speaker lists traits that resonated personally—dismissing praise as luck, isolating while remote, and setting unreachable standards—plus how dismissive coworkers, interruptions, and comparisons intensify those feelings.

Research cited in the talk notes limited formal studies, higher reported rates among women of color, trans women, and women in male-dominated fields, and executive survey figures on silence at work. The narrative moves through childhood, school, and IT examples where authority figures undermined confidence, then asks whether recovery is ongoing rather than permanent.

Practical guidance emphasizes changing unsupportive jobs, joining peer groups such as WiCyS mentor circles, learning new domains without expecting omniscience, asking for help, setting small stretch goals, and pushing back when others ignore contributions. Homework invites listeners to list concrete comfort-zone steps. The close urges knowing niche worth, tolerating failure, and surrounding oneself with people who reinforce capability.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2022-Anuradha Modi-Pentesting Android Applications-Lab Setup to Get Started
talks.teaser: Walks through building an Android pentesting lab and the first static and dynamic checks against a sample app.
talks.summary:
The talk is an introduction to penetration testing Android applications for people starting out in mobile security. The speaker explains why mobile apps matter given how many people carry smartphones, and why devices often hold sensitive data behind weak lock screens. The session splits testing into dynamic analysis, which observes an app while it runs, and static analysis, which examines the decompiled package.

For the lab, the speaker walks through a set of tools: Android Studio, the Android Debug Bridge, Genymotion virtual devices, a deliberately vulnerable sample app, and Burp Suite as an intercepting proxy. The setup covers installing the sample app on an emulated device, pointing it at a host-side server, routing device traffic through Burp, and importing the Burp CA certificate so HTTPS traffic can be captured. A captured login request shows the traffic path working.

For static analysis, the speaker reviews the manifest for settings such as the backup and debuggable flags and for unnecessary permissions. Exported activities can be launched directly with an adb command to reach screens without logging in. Converting the DEX code to a JAR and browsing it in a Java decompiler can expose hard-coded credentials and API keys. The talk closes with OWASP learning resources and an offer to help with lab configuration.
