talks.title: Diana Initiative 2022-Ana Trueba-Monitoring Global Data Privacy Developments through OSINT
talks.teaser: Shows a privacy officer's process for setting up keyword and social feed trackers to follow global data protection changes.
talks.summary:
The talk addresses how hard it is to keep up with privacy and data protection changes that arrive at once from national, regional, state, sector-specific and court sources. The speaker, a privacy compliance manager who also serves as a data protection officer for a software company working across Latin America, presents open source intelligence as a way to have relevant developments reach the practitioner instead of reacting ad hoc. Information is grouped into media, internet publications, government sources, professional and academic work, commercial literature and grey literature.

The method follows a Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle with an added diagnosis stage. In diagnosis, the speaker reviews internal privacy documents and turns them into guiding questions and a short list of keywords, aiming for 10 to 12, which become trackers pairing a topic with the people or organisations discussing it. For planning, the speaker suggests two or three sources per keyword and no more than five. Examples include curated Twitter lists of regulators and privacy experts, social listening tools such as TweetDeck to test whether keywords match real conversation, RSS feeds read through Feedly, and Google Alerts.

The check stage asks whether the setup reduces workload, whether regulations and enforcement actions are being caught, and whether the chosen terms actually appear online, since some regional terminology differs from the English term. Adjustments follow from those answers. The closing lessons are that simple, well-configured tools beat complex ones, most options are free or have free tiers, tracking should run from a dedicated account, and reviews should happen weekly or at least every two weeks with fixed storage locations.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2022-Kassandra L. Pierre-Threat Modeling your Mental Health
talks.teaser: Maps threat-modeling habits onto mental wellness so practitioners can spot stressors, gauge impact, and scale coping plans.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by connecting crisis-intervention and threat-intelligence mindsets, then frames recent workplace and community stress as risks that demand deliberate planning rather than improvisation. The speaker cites population and industry statistics on stress, burnout, and retention pressure in security roles, and names recurring stressors such as long hours, certification grind, exclusion, and cultures that reward overwork.

The core method treats personal well-being like a system with known weak points. Attendees are guided through self-check questions, brief daily journaling, and identifying personal triggers and tactics. The talk parallels organizational threat modeling with recognizing vulnerabilities, assessing impact, and choosing countermeasures, including building a support network, scheduling preventative wellness, and using benefits such as employee assistance programs, PTO, and telehealth.

The close covers escalation signals such as mood rating trends and when to involve clinicians, plus crisis resources. A downloadable template and resource list are offered so listeners can draft their own wellness threat model and maintain it over time.

talks.title: StreamYard A/V Backstage and Greenroom walkthrough
talks.teaser: Volunteers learn StreamYard green-room AV checks, studio queue, always-live broadcast, overlays, and emcee coordination.
talks.summary:
Conference volunteers who sign up for audio-visual or green-room shifts need a practical way to run StreamYard without accidentally going on air too early or dropping speakers mid-transition. The presentation walks through logging in with two-factor authentication, entering the studio queue, and using admin features such as backstage messages while speakers wait.

For green-room duty, the flow emphasizes confirming audio, video, and slide sharing— including when to guide someone to the share icon versus using Google Slides direct share versus full screen share for animations, videos, or speaker notes. On the production side, operators use layout controls for one or two speakers and presentations, start a continuous “go live” broadcast at the shift start, apply sponsor and event overlays between talks, and coordinate timing through private chat with emcees and speakers.

The session contrasts last year’s end-broadcast-between-talks model with a always-live approach where everyone is removed off-screen between segments instead. It covers bringing up MC segments (including dual mode for sponsor slides), sequencing presentation then speaker, supporting Q&A via the emcee, and ending the broadcast only at shift handoffs such as lunch.

talks.title: How to join TDI Discord
talks.teaser: A walkthrough covers Discord signup, invite links, and bots that verify email, rules, and captcha DMs for The Diana Initiative server.
talks.summary:
The session targets attendees who want access to The Diana Initiative Discord but may be new to the platform or stuck behind gates. It begins with installing Discord from the website, creating an account or signing in, and using an invitation URL when the client does not prompt for a server automatically.

Once inside, automated messages from Carlbot and Wickbot block full channel visibility until verification finishes. The presenter walks through confirming email, accepting terms, submitting the verify action, and completing a captcha delivered by direct message. If the bot message never arrives, the talk points to privacy settings that must allow DMs from server members.

After verification, attendee and sponsor rooms become visible. The closing notes explain using the ticket system on the left for general support, role requests such as speaker or sponsor labels, or reporting code of conduct issues.

talks.title: Diana Initiative StreamYard Virtual Speaker Wrangler / MC 2022 walk-through
talks.teaser: Shows virtual wranglers how to use Stream Yard backstage, share sponsors, hand off to speakers, and manage Discord Q&A.
talks.summary:
The recording walks through what a virtual speaker wrangler does before and during a streamed talk on Stream Yard. The presenter joins the backstage link, allows camera and microphone access, enters a queue, and explains that nobody sees wranglers until AV adds them to the live program, so they should not mute unnecessarily while waiting.

Inside the studio, the wrangler shares sponsor logos from supplied slides or via screen sharing, then tells AV in private chat when both wrangler and speaker are ready. On air, they thank sponsors, mention related event items such as a career village panel, a sponsor raffle, and later social activities, introduce the upcoming speaker, and exit once AV switches to the talk.

The closing segment covers question handling: watching the Discord Q&A channel, warning speakers when no questions appear, and either reading questions aloud or forwarding them in private chat according to speaker preference. A short note touches on what to do when unsure how to pronounce a speaker’s name.

talks.title: Diana Initiative StreamYard Virtual Speaker 2022 walk-through
talks.teaser: Shows virtual speakers how to join, share slides and handle questions on a streaming platform.
talks.summary:
This organizer walkthrough prepares presenters for a virtual speaking slot on a streaming platform. It starts with a test link that asks for a display name, which can be a handle rather than a legal name. Presenters first join a green room to check their microphone and screen sharing, then enter the live studio about ten minutes before their slot. Until the presenter goes live, they sit in a queue where no one can see or hear them.

Once backstage, presenters can share either a slide deck, which advances for everyone, or their full screen, which works well when two people present from one deck. The video recommends using private chat rather than public comments, since public comments appear on the event's YouTube channel. Speakers should keep speaker notes and private chat on a second screen, and signal readiness in private chat so the MC can introduce them.

Near the end, a speaker wrangler passes along audience questions. Presenters should repeat each question aloud so the recording and viewers on the stream who are not in the Discord can follow. When time runs out, questions may stop, and presenters can close the browser tab to leave or be removed if they run over.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2021-Diana Nores-Cyberpuffs at 40+
talks.teaser: Explores how professionals over forty can pivot into cybersecurity by leveraging life experience, soft skills, and community support.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens from an educator’s angle, linking Powerpuff-era encouragement for students to the speaker’s own move into security and privacy work after years in education. Workforce data frames the gap: women are often cited as roughly a fifth to a quarter of the field, while a large share of IT roles stay open and only a small fraction of those seats go to women. Reports on degrees, age cohorts, and career changers underline that many entrants are young graduates, and that mature women who switch careers remain a thin slice.

The middle contrasts fresh graduates who may lack soft skills with seasoned professionals who bring collaboration and leadership but need technical depth. The speaker catalogs transferable strengths—creative problem-solving, patience with siloed systems, planning and “what-if” thinking, communication, adaptability, and sustained curiosity—and ties persistence to passion rather than salary alone. Practical paths include self-driven research, free online training with certification tracks, mentors, and conferences and groups such as the Diana Initiative.

The close stresses projection and advocacy: encouraging women at every age toward technology, mentorship at all levels, explicit organizational diversity targets, and networking for emotional support as well as career pointers. A shared resource board collects programs and communities, with emphasis on paying forward help once you are established.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2021-Megan Daudelin-Soft Skills in a Hard World: Why Your Innate Strengths Should
talks.teaser: Argues that communication, analysis, and adaptability deserve equal weight with certifications in security hiring and career growth.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by acknowledging that security culture often glorifies deeply technical hobbyists—CTF competitors, home labs, endless certifications—while people who excel at synthesis, communication, and structured thinking can feel like imposters. She traces her own path from digital forensics through enterprise security, content development, curriculum design, and consulting, stressing that recurring technical retraining never matched what made her effective or fulfilled.

The middle contrasts buzzword soft skills in job postings with how interviews still center awkward behavioral prompts and yes-or-no technical checks. Teams that hire for curiosity, collaboration, and resilience outperform those obsessed with unicorn requirement lists; misaligned roles drain people even when the technology is learnable. She ties self-knowledge to concrete preferences—clear tasks, turning scattered data into narratives, teaching and editing for varied audiences—and notes parallels in hobbies like reading, cooking, and structured games.

She closes with practical guidance: map innate strengths beyond the office, reshape unstructured work with personal structure, and in interviews admit knowledge gaps while linking adjacent experience and eagerness to learn. Job requirements should state minimum technical baselines; employers should recruit for adaptability and team-fit skills that improve satisfaction, retention, and inclusion.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2021-Vidya Murthy-Why non-technicals matter
talks.teaser: Argues that non-technical roles fill a large share of cybersecurity jobs and strengthen defenses through business-aligned risk thinking.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens from the perspective of a chief operating officer in medical device security who built a career without a coding background. A familiar conference moment—being told that breaking in requires learning to code—frames a wider problem: newcomers often believe cybersecurity is only hoodies and terminals, yet industry surveys cited in the talk place roughly thirty percent of roles outside deeply technical work, spanning governance, project management, analytics, technical writing, and privacy regulation.

The middle develops that argument with organizational and product examples. Homogeneous teams can miss human and clinical context, illustrated by a widely discussed health-app design gap and by hospital devices that must stay safe for patients when component vulnerabilities appear. A rough review of large medical device vendors finds non-technical leaders guiding product security in many cases. Hiring trends and studies are used to show job descriptions shifting toward problem-solving and cross-functional expertise rather than multi-page technical checklists.

The close focuses on practical ways non-technical staff prove value: translating security issues into business risk, using risk-based prioritization, partnering across functions, and strengthening communication, program management, and strategic acumen while learning enough technical vocabulary to collaborate—not to become developers. Listeners are urged to inventory their strengths, network, and treat diversity of thought as defensive strength.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2021-Bishakha Jain-Manifesting and Mastering the art of Executive Presence
talks.teaser: Offers practical tips on posture, voice, storytelling and on-camera presence to build executive presence in security careers.
talks.summary:
Bishakha Jain opens with her own path, from a remote region with little IT activity to a penetration testing role and later an MBA in cyber security. Her argument is that competence alone does not carry someone up the career ladder, and that confidence and warmth are what make people trust a leader. She presents executive presence as a set of habits that can be practised rather than a trait someone is born with, and she points to public figures whose distinctive styles made them memorable.

The middle of the talk covers concrete habits. Posture shapes how seriously people are taken, and hand gestures, pauses, a steady voice and fewer filler words all affect perception. She suggests recording yourself on a phone to spot filler words, preparing several layers of depth on any topic so that questions do not catch you out, and controlling facial expression under pressure. For clothing and surroundings she advises choosing what feels authentic and keeping a calm, uncluttered background. For video calls she argues for keeping the camera on, using fewer slides, and turning off notifications to protect personal information.

In the question round she adds that storytelling helps explain security to non-specialists, that outlining content before building slides saves effort, and that makeup is optional if it does not suit you. The takeaway is that small daily changes build a reputation for credibility that holds up in high-stakes moments.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2021-Grace Chi-"See" TI - Behind the Curtains for Cyber Threat Intelligence Careers
talks.teaser: Explores cyber threat intelligence fundamentals, career paths, and practical resources for newcomers entering the field.
talks.summary:
The session opens by framing why cyber threat intelligence matters in modern security and how career pivots often pass through uninformed optimism, informed pessimism, and burnout before reaching steady contribution. The speaker defines CTI using established industry language, separates intelligence from merely hoarding feeds or indicators, and cites survey trends showing wider organizational adoption over recent years.

The middle walks through where CTI teams sit in vendors, government, consulting, and enterprise settings, why the role is rarely entry-level, and which skills transfer from SOC, incident response, engineering, or nontraditional backgrounds. She explains the intelligence cycle—planning, collection, processing, analysis, and dissemination—with a small personal phishing-link example, then contrasts low-budget, fragmented, and mature program models plus how platforms and spreadsheets fit operational workflows.

The close focuses on hiring realities, networking stories, reading and thanking researchers, communities such as the Diana Initiative, and curated free resources including Awesome Threat Intelligence and SANS CTI summit recordings. Listeners leave with a vocabulary foundation, realistic expectations about specialization, and concrete next steps to learn tools, frameworks, and sharing practices without treating intelligence as set-and-forget.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2021-Chesleah Kribs & Marisa Midler & Destiney Plaza-Let's Crack Passwords
talks.teaser: Shows how John the Ripper and Hashcat crack captured password hashes, then covers passphrases and password managers.
talks.summary:
The session opens with common password mistakes: reuse, notes stuck to monitors, personal details such as pet names, and default credentials. The presenters frame the attacker's view by working through a Kali Linux toolset. They stress checking authorization before any cracking, then load a common wordlist, identify an unknown hash type with a hash identifier tool, and run John the Ripper against sample MD5 and SHA-256 hashes, including a run limited to one user.

Next they repeat the workflow with Hashcat, covering attack modes, benchmarking and combination attacks. They then pull hashes from a deliberately vulnerable web application backed by MySQL, using a manual SQL injection, and crack them with both tools. Two further scenarios follow: one starts from an exposed CMS admin panel that leaks SHA-1 hashes, and one is a Windows path where anonymous SMB access leads to a service account hash that cracks almost instantly. Other crackers such as rainbow table tools, CrackStation, Hydra and Medusa are briefly listed.

The closing section argues for passphrases over short complex passwords, avoiding reuse, and using a password manager to generate unique credentials. The presenters note that manager choice depends on risk posture and on cloud versus locally hosted options. The main takeaway is that length and uniqueness matter most, and that cracking should only be done with written permission in legal lab environments.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2021-Charu Bansal-Navigating the Imposter Syndrome
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Diana Initiative 2021-Charu Bansal-Navigating the Imposter Syndrome.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk at the Diana Initiative 2021, Charu Bansal shares her personal journey and practical strategies for navigating imposter syndrome within the cybersecurity industry. Transitioning from a liberal arts background with no formal technical education to serving as an Information Systems Security Officer (ISSO) for a global enterprise, Bansal addresses the pervasive feeling of inadequacy often experienced in technical environments. She highlights why the condition cannot simply be permanently cured, framing it instead as an ongoing navigation process, and provides actionable advice for both individuals facing imposter syndrome and mentors supporting them.

### Key Topics
- **Personal Background and Transition:** Growing up in rural Himalayas with limited access to technology, Bansal pivoted from liberal arts into security seven years prior when a team took a chance on her. Her early days involved learning foundational terms like penetration testing, man-in-the-middle, and Burp Suite while navigating underrepresentation as one of few women at technical conferences.
- **Knowledge vs. Intelligence:** Bansal emphasizes that not knowing specific jargon, tools, or acronyms does not indicate a lack of intelligence. Intelligence is the capacity to learn, and technical knowledge can be acquired through self-directed study, security podcasts, newsletters, community meetups, and conferences.
- **Rejecting Limiting Boxes:** She cautions against allowing colleagues to pigeonhole individuals into non-technical administrative tasks (e.g., solely taking meeting notes or maintaining Confluence pages) under the assumption that they cannot handle technical or engineering discussions.
- **Non-Technical Strengths in Security:** Security is inherently rooted in human behavior, not merely technical problems. Bansal discusses how non-traditional backgrounds provide critical perspectives in threat modeling, cross-border payment platforms, incident response planning, and creative phishing exercises through an understanding of international laws, cultural differences, and life experiences.
- **Mentorship and Support:** Effective mentoring requires genuine dialogue to understand a mentee's exact knowledge gaps rather than overwhelming them with generic resources (such as lengthy course lists or extensive GitHub links) or doing the work for them.

### Technical Details
- **Threat Modeling Integration:** Threat modeling is highlighted as a collaborative exercise aimed at identifying and proactively mitigating potential threats to systems, processes, or applications. Bansal illustrates how life experiences—such as anticipating what could go wrong when moving across continents—translate directly into threat modeling frameworks, including evaluating payment methods and threat vectors on a global payment platform.
- **Human Factors in Incident Planning:** Non-technical domain expertise, including familiarity with multi-jurisdictional legal and regulatory requirements, contributes directly to incident response planning, while behavioral insights inform anti-phishing simulations.

### Takeaways
- **Normalize Asking for Help:** Imposter syndrome thrives when individuals hide their struggles out of fear of exposure. The security community must normalize admitting knowledge gaps and asking for guidance.
- **Show Up Prepared:** When faced with intimidating meetings, demand an agenda, research unfamiliar terms beforehand, and continuously show up and listen attentively even if only a fraction of the discussion is immediately understood.
- **Guidance for Mentors:** Mentors should prioritize targeted teaching over fixing issues for mentees, avoiding resource overload and establishing mutual trust through targeted questions.
- **Internal Affirmation:** Acknowledge your accomplishments and bravery in challenging established industry biases, reframing self-doubt with the reminder that diverse perspectives provide vital security value.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2021-Rebecca Hoffart-Spark a Journey: Inspiring Girls to Find Pathways to the ...
talks.teaser: Shows how a teacher drew girls and underrepresented students into cybersecurity through camps, competitions and clubs.
talks.summary:
Rebecca Hoffart, a computer science teacher in the US Virgin Islands, opens with the island's context: a small population, child poverty, damage from the 2017 hurricanes, and COVID-era school disruptions that cut into students' time in class. She presents outreach as a way to build a local cybersecurity pipeline for young people who would otherwise have few routes into the field.

She traces how her work grew from a cyber camp she attended in 2014. Early camps drew mostly boys, so she partnered with a YWCA program, a community computer center, the local university and a girls-in-ICT fair to bring in more girls. An all-girls CyberPatriot team formed in 2016, and several of those students later went on to university cyber programs or earned a national award. Later camps brought in local women as instructors, and a girls who code club started after the hurricanes.

She ends with the approaches she found most effective: competitions such as CyberPatriot, picoCTF and CyberStart; hands-on tools like Scratch, Raspberry Pi, Lego and tablets, even for very young children; and letting older students teach younger ones, which built their confidence. Her takeaways are to learn, mentor, inspire and never give up.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2021-Duane Dunston-Mentoring and Training Experts: A cognitive science approach
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Diana Initiative 2021-Duane Dunston-Mentoring and Training Experts: A cognitive science approach.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Dwayne Dunston, an associate professor of cyber security at Champlain College with 24+ years of industry experience, presents a cognitive science approach to mentoring and training cybersecurity experts. This talk is a follow-up to his previous Diana Initiative presentation, addressing concerns about scalability raised by an audience member.

## Key Concepts
Dunston distinguishes between novices (those new to a domain who rely on critical thinking, problem-solving, and mimicking) and experts (those with domain-specific knowledge). He introduces the Expert Reversal Effect from cognitive load theory: methods effective for training novices can actually be detrimental to experts because they may undo long-term schemas already built up, especially in graded educational settings.

## Training Experts Through Deliberate Practice
Unlike novices who need structured instruction, experts need coaching and advice rather than feedback. Dunston defines deliberate practice as repetitive, willful attempts to improve performance—distinguishing it from general practice. He emphasizes that quality of experience matters far more than hours spent; 24 years of experience provides less expertise development than focused deliberate practice on specific weaknesses.

Key principles for expert development include:
- **Dynamic Practice**: Mentors must know their mentees well enough to adjust difficulty levels, progressively pushing them to apply skills in new contexts
- **Mentor-Mentee Relationship**: Regular check-ins and communication enable correction of mistakes and refinement of weak skills
- **Cognitive Apprenticeship**: The mentor makes thinking visible, provides feedback, allows reflection, and observes the mentee's work

## Practical Methods
Dunston illustrates his approach through his own experience learning Mitre ATT&CK Cyber Threat Intelligence. Rather than self-study, he engaged a mentor who provided threat intelligence reports for him to map against the framework, met regularly for guided feedback and advice, and progressively tackled harder scenarios across different domains (universities, industrial control systems).

For training providers, he recommends:
- **Case Studies**: Recreate real industry incidents from fire eye or Mandiant reports and have students solve them before reviewing the expert solution
- **Community-Driven Hard Problems**: Establish databases of hard problems across threat hunting, incident response, threat intelligence, and reverse engineering. Example: Honeynet Project's approach of posting attack PCAPs for community analysis and expert review
- **Worked Examples**: Show step-by-step how to perform tasks rather than directing learners to "google it"

## Takeaways
Mentoring experts requires understanding individual needs and capabilities. While some aspects of novice training apply to experts (particularly worked examples), the emphasis shifts to coaching, deliberate practice on specific weak areas, and progressive difficulty increases. A community database of hard problems could enable experts to pursue deliberate practice in their specific skill gaps, addressing the scalability concern from the previous year's talk.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2021-Veronica Schmitt-If we do not have it we should build it
talks.teaser: Five design philosophies show teams how to build application logs for incident response and early compromise detection.
talks.summary:
Organizations often discover breaches with almost no usable telemetry: VPN, firewall, and SIEM data may be missing while endpoint logs are cleared, which leaves responders reconstructing events from scraps. The speaker draws on enterprise incident work and hands-on forensics on medical devices, where maintenance and debug output exists but security audit trails rarely do. Without correlated evidence, claiming that nothing was compromised is not supportable.

The middle of the talk argues that security arrives too late in the software lifecycle and that developers, defenders, and testers need a shared view of what logs must capture. Motivated by NIST controls, CIS Critical Control 6, and OWASP ASVS logging guidance, the speaker built a spreadsheet benchmark (headed toward a web tool) to score log maturity and fit checks into unit testing. Engaging development teams borrows DevOps narratives from The Phoenix Project and The Unicorn Project, emphasizing psychological safety and customer focus rather than blame after incidents.

Practitioners hear five philosophies: keep logs simple, structured, and purpose-driven; tag sensitive fields and metadata; control logging debt sprint by sprint; design for inevitable compromise with traceable workflows; and treat storage, transport, and access with skepticism. The talk also points to OWASP Cornucopia for developer threat modeling and recurring review of legacy logs that leak secrets. The takeaway is to treat logging as a product feature early so SIEM ingestion, early detection, and root cause analysis are possible instead of waiting hundreds of days for external notice.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2021-Terra Cooke-Let's Simplify NIST 800-53: Turning Everyone's Favorite
talks.teaser: Explains the NIST 800-53 control families in plain language and shows how each one appears in everyday work.
talks.summary:
Terra Cooke walks through NIST SP 800-53, the framework of security and privacy controls used heavily in federal systems, aimed at people who are new to security or audit. She explains that the revision she covers groups its controls into roughly 20 to 25 families, and she argues that most people in security and engineering touch these families every day even if they never name them.

She goes through the families one at a time, giving her own plain definition for each and an everyday comparison. Access control is framed as asking who has access, whether that access is valid, and why it exists, with least privilege and restricted access as examples. Audit and accountability is about who did what and when, illustrated with apartment maintenance logs. Configuration management is compared to an HOA approval process that keeps changes uniform against a baseline. Contingency planning is presented as the response when normal operations are disrupted, with the recent pandemic cited. Other families get the same treatment, including media protection, physical and environmental protection, personnel security, PII processing, risk assessment and supply chain risk management.

In the question round, she suggested that a team without a GRC function should first work out what matters most to the business and its industry, then model controls around that. She pointed to the NIST Cybersecurity Framework as a good starting point and the Risk Management Framework as a more thorough option. She argued that the framework matters less than whether it fits the organization, and said "safeguards" might be a friendlier word than "controls".

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2021-Cathy Gellis-Section 230: The Law That Everyone Loves to Hate, And What It
talks.teaser: Explains how Section 230 shields online platforms from user-content liability, its exceptions, and why the speaker wants it kept.
talks.summary:
The talk explains Section 230 of the US Communications Decency Act, the provision that stops online services from being treated as the publisher of content their users post. It argues that much of the public anger aimed at the law is really aimed at the internet itself. The history starts in the mid-1990s, when a New York court ruling against an early commercial online service pushed Congress to act, and the speaker shows how the provision survived after the rest of the decency act was struck down.

The statute's core idea is that whoever created the content stays responsible for it, while the service that carried it is protected. The breadth of that protection covers social platforms, review sites, comment sections, search engines, email and internet providers, and even individuals who run a blog. The talk walks through the carve-outs: intellectual property claims fall under the copyright safe harbors, which the speaker describes as conditional and expensive to litigate, and federal criminal law is also excluded. The speaker says a later law aimed at sex trafficking led some services to drop lawful adult offerings, leaving sex workers in more dangerous conditions.

In the closing discussion, the speaker says the law works through incentives rather than penalties, and that algorithmic recommendations resemble a bookstore choosing its stock, which does not forfeit protection. Questions on moderation at scale, competition, and government pressure on platforms were addressed. The takeaway is that the law should be left largely alone, apart from removing the intellectual property exemption and rolling back that later law.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2021-Breanne Boland-The System Call Is Coming from Inside the House: Appsec Horror
talks.teaser: Walks through common appsec mistakes told as horror stories, from stale dependencies to overly broad cloud permissions.
talks.summary:
Breanne Boland frames common application security mistakes as a set of horror-themed monsters. Each one is a familiar way teams invite trouble while trying to do the right thing. Examples include automatic updates that pull in a breaking change, which the speaker traced to a dependency update that broke servers until it was pinned to an earlier version, and free browser extensions that changed hands and became malicious.

Other monsters cover verbose logs and stack traces that expose internal details, secrets stored in code even in private repositories, and input validation applied only in the browser. The speaker recommends proper secret storage, commit checks for secrets and debug output, and validation on both client and server. Legacy software such as old WordPress or Windows installs persists because rewrites are expensive, and overly broad AWS IAM permissions tend to stay in place as teams grow, so roles should be split early and tightened over time.

The closing advice is about people as much as code. Make security easy to work with so colleagues bring problems forward instead of hiding them, reward those who report issues, write clearly for non-technical readers, and have someone other than the author review changes, since authors cannot see their own work objectively.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2021-Harpreet Mangat-Shifting to Purple: A high-level overview on Purple Teaming
talks.teaser: Gives an overview of building a purple team, covering its benefits and an eight-step framework for running joint exercises.
talks.summary:
The talk explains purple teaming as a way to go beyond separate red and blue teams by bringing them together with other groups, such as threat intelligence and server specialists. The speaker stresses that the mix of teams depends on each organization, and that exercises can run ad hoc or on a quarterly or yearly schedule.

The benefits are grouped into technology, people and process. On the technology side, joint exercises can improve detection, help close gaps quickly after a red team finding that needs only a small configuration change, and produce a roadmap for future tool purchases. For people, pooling specialists builds communication and a shared culture instead of rivalry. For process, exercises test the blue team's defenses and connect technical results to management reporting.

The speaker then outlines an eight-step framework: planning, creating a structure, communicating with the teams involved, training, collaborating, maintaining documentation, leading the team, and providing ongoing support. Planning includes choosing metrics that tie findings to CIS controls, MITRE, or risk ratings. The exercise flow runs from preparation through testing, gap mapping, reporting and retesting. The talk closes by urging continuous feedback, change logs, and a designated owner for documentation and metrics.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2021-Rachel Harpley-OPSEC & OSINT to HACK your JOB HUNT
talks.teaser: Shows how OPSEC and OSINT methods can guide a job search through networking, recruiter types and tracking outreach.
talks.summary:
Rachel Harpley opens by treating a job hunt as a system to analyse. She borrows the OPSEC process of identifying critical information, analysing threats and vulnerabilities, assessing risk and applying countermeasures, and applies it to the candidate. Her point is that a person's skills, social media presence and career history are the information that recruiters and hiring managers will examine, so a resume, LinkedIn profile and online persona should tell one clear and consistent story. She illustrates this with a career changer whose mixed sales and recruiting experience raised doubts, and with an employer who found a salesperson's local news coverage in a quick web search before making an offer.

The middle of the talk covers the people and organisations on the other side. She separates corporate talent acquisition recruiters, who screen for culture fit and minimum requirements, from agency recruiters, who may act more freely in a candidate's interest. She contrasts technical and non-technical hiring managers, and large enterprises with small and mid-sized firms, which differ in risk tolerance, process and willingness to hire entry-level staff. OSINT is presented as a research habit: documenting which companies, teams and hiring managers fit a target profile, and tracking outreach with a simple log and small daily goals.

She ends with networking advice. Good outreach uses several touch points, such as engaging with a public post before sending a short, specific request, and then reciprocating help. She mentions bots, feeds and alerts as ways to monitor hiring-manager updates, and answers audience questions on job titles, icebreakers and interview research. Her takeaway is that networking often returns more for the time spent than mass online applications, though applying online still makes sense when a candidate has spare time.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2021-Simran Kathpalia & Namitha S-Dissecting Go and Rust binaries
talks.teaser: Shows how compiled Go and Rust programs look when dissected, starting from a basic hello world build.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at what Go and Rust programs contain once they have been compiled into binaries. It opens with a basic introduction to programming languages, covering what a systems-oriented language is and how source code becomes a compiled program. Memory management is touched on as one of the topics that separates these languages.

The presenters then use a simple hello world program as a concrete starting point. They walk through the compiled output, looking at the main function and the functions that are called from it, and how those calls can be followed inside the binary. The walkthrough stays at a introductory level, so the discussion of individual compiler output details is limited to the basic structure described here.

For a practitioner, the main takeaway is a method for approaching an unfamiliar compiled Go or Rust file: find the program's entry point and trace how functions are invoked from it. The talk is aimed at people who want a first look at reading these binaries.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2021-Megan Carney-Bobbing for Apples: Developing alerts for macOS
talks.teaser: Walks through custom macOS detections for persistence, quarantine removal and scripting abuse, plus tuning them in practice.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that macOS endpoints are often under-monitored because their security tooling is less mature than on Windows, and that a compromised Mac can still serve as a foothold into the wider network. Custom alerting is presented as a way to cover the choke points attackers depend on, such as persistence mechanisms, and to tune detections to an organization's own environment and appetite for risk.

The speaker then walks through alerts that worked in her environment. These cover SUID binaries appearing on disk, new root certificates being installed, user-level launch agents that call scripting languages, crontab edits, doc replacement persistence, removal of the quarantine attribute with xattr, processes launched from library scripts, python parenting openssl or osascript, and deletion of unified logs. OSQuery is suggested for several of these checks, and adware running with root privileges is treated as a real risk rather than a nuisance.

The closing advice centers on working with incident responders and engineering teams, since alerts that generate false positives get ignored and must be tested and tuned after rollout. Newcomers are encouraged to start with persistence locations, common malware behaviors such as curl downloads that skip quarantine, and scripting activity, and to alert on anything outside a known baseline.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2021-Khoa Nguyen & Scott Riese-Making It Real: Turning an Attack Chain Into a CTF
talks.teaser: Shows how a real red team attack chain was rebuilt as a month-long capture the flag for internal staff.
talks.summary:
The talk explains how a Microsoft red team turned one of its own attack chains into an internal capture the flag. The goal was to let staff practise attacks in tools they use daily, not abstract puzzles. The original chain began with one compromised Azure DevOps personal access token, which allowed a malicious build task to be injected into a pipeline. The release process then pushed the backdoored binary to build and developer machines, compromising over 7000 machines.

The CTF started players on the corporate network under an assumed-breach model, with three entry points: a vulnerable web app, an Active Directory domain and an Azure DevOps organization. Reconnaissance flags set the scope first. The 25 challenges spanned four categories and unlocked progressively. Examples included a pipeline edit that printed a flag on a build server, a path traversal that exposed an application config file, and a token-tampering challenge where a changed username claim in a bearer token granted admin access due to weak validation. The pilot ran on CTFd for about a month, with weekly write-ups.

Problems appeared quickly: players copied pipelines, which did not carry the secrets they needed, and others watched successful runs to lift flags, so the team scripted removal of recent runs. Of 36 registered players, 35 completed at least one challenge and three finished all 25. The main takeaways were to lock down build pipelines and repositories, validate tokens properly and isolate the exercise environment.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2021-Julie Carres-A N00bHacker's Guide to the Infosec Galaxy
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Diana Initiative 2021-Julie Carres-A N00bHacker's Guide to the Infosec Galaxy.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this Diana Initiative 2021 session, speaker Julie Carres—a math teacher with an art history degree who transitioned into infosec via DEF CON and was accepted into the SANS Women's Immersion Academy—delivers a comprehensive guide for beginners ("noobs") looking to learn information security. Emphasizing that reading dense technical books late at night after work can be exhausting, Carres advocates for gamified, hands-on learning aligned with personal learning styles to keep self-study engaging and sustainable.

### Key Topics
- **Learning Archetypes (Alice vs. Jill):** Carres categorizes learners into two profiles based on how they explore topics:
  - *Alice (Deep Dive Specialist):* Tends to go down rabbit holes, demanding to understand underlying mechanics completely before moving on. Alices benefit from resources that push them to broaden their scope across multiple disciplines rather than getting stuck on a single challenge or topic.
  - *Jill (Broad Generalist):* Curious about everything, skims many topics, and is quick to experiment, but risks lacking deep foundational knowledge. Jills benefit from structured curriculums that force them to narrow their focus and follow paths through to completion.
- **Capture the Flag (CTF) Platforms:** CTFs provide structured, low-pressure, gamified learning environments that cater to both archetypes:
  - *TryHackMe:* Features guided learning paths (such as complete beginner tracks, web security, and offensive pentesting), succinct modular lessons, and in-browser VMs/attack boxes.
  - *PicoCTF:* Created by Carnegie Mellon, offering jeopardy-style challenges covering cryptography, binary exploitation, web exploitation, and more across varied difficulty levels with built-in web shells.
  - *OverTheWire:* War game site (notably the Bandit track) focused on practical Linux command-line skills, SSH, and search methodology using a repetitive, scaffolding pedagogical approach.
  - *SANS Holiday Hack Challenge:* An annually updated, MMO-style puzzle environment with avatars, narrative quests, and community write-ups available after winners are announced.
- **Learning to Code:** While not every infosec role requires development experience, familiarity with scripting, web technologies, or reverse engineering concepts is highly valuable. Recommended pathways range from academic courses (edX CS50, Coursera Princeton Java, Georgia Tech Python) to gamified interactive tools (Scratch block coding, CodeCombat RPG, and Codecademy).
- **Crypto Challenges & "Chall" Sites:** Static challenge resources like Rank.org, NewbieContest.org, NotPron, and US Cyber Command Valentine's Day crypto challenges provide puzzles that test mathematical reasoning, cryptography, and problem-solving without easily accessible answer keys.
- **Projects and Family Engagement:** Practical suggestions for applying skills and demonstrating aptitude without a formal tech resume include writing technical blog posts/write-ups, setting up home lab hypervisors with VulnHub machines, configuring a network-wide ad-blocking Pi-hole, and engaging family members through Scratch Jr, cryptographic scavenger hunts, or CyberStart America.

### Technical Details
- **CTF Fundamentals:** Digital security competitions revolving around locating hidden text strings ("flags"), typically enclosed in curly brackets and often written in leetspeak.
- **Linux CLI Mastery:** OverTheWire's Bandit builds essential terminal skills incrementally (connecting via `ssh`, exploring directories with `ls`, finding files, inspecting permissions) where the output of one level serves as the credential for the next.
- **Home Networking & DNS:** Running a Raspberry Pi-hole serves as a hands-on project to learn local DNS configuration, network traffic troubleshooting, and basic server management.

### Takeaways
- Align study resources with personal tendencies: "Alices" need structure to broaden their perspective, while "Jills" need curriculums to maintain depth and focus.
- Gamified platforms and write-up walkthroughs provide safe, accessible environments to reverse-engineer solutions when stuck.
- Developing a technical blog and documenting CTF write-ups or hands-on home projects acts as an effective portfolio for career transitions into infosec.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2021-Douglas Brush-You Don't Have to Be Crazy to Work Here: An honest talk about...
talks.teaser: Explores burnout, anxiety, and stigma in information security, pairing personal recovery with practical workplace and self-care guidance.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by framing how security practitioners protect systems while often neglecting their own psychological well-being, citing industry stress surveys, long hours, and unhealthy coping patterns tied to conference culture and always-on roles. He offers trigger warnings, clarifies he is not providing medical advice, and defines mental health, self-care, and neurodiversity as context for why stigma keeps people from seeking help.

The middle follows his path from adolescent panic attacks through entrepreneurial burnout, a disabling injury, job loss, and a severe depressive crisis scored on a life-stress inventory, then describes medication, acceptance and commitment therapy, boundary-setting such as removing work alerts from his phone, morning routines, and distinguishing real self-care from harmful substitutes. He ties these choices to building a more resilient consulting practice where healthier staff reportedly improved retention and business outcomes.

He closes with workplace actions: open dialogue, mindful language, parity between mental and physical illness, compassionate listening without dismissal, calling out stigmatizing behavior, and a simple homework exercise to list five personal strengths each morning. Practitioners should treat operator wellness as ongoing operations work, not a personal failing to hide.

talks.teaser: Maps shared lessons between cyber defense and diversity work through identity, privilege, access, and organizational culture.
talks.summary:
The presenter frames security and diversity, equity, and inclusion as fields that face strikingly similar sustained-focus problems, truisms, and cultural barriers, using a playful adversary dialogue to argue that homogeneous thinking makes defenses predictable. After noting that meaningful change requires participation beyond specialist teams and a clear sense of why change matters, the talk stresses that DEI work carries distinct historical weight that must not be flattened into security analogies.

The core of the session compares how identity, privilege, and access are understood in information security versus in inclusion work, drawing on ideas such as least privilege, privilege escalation, bounded awareness, and who controls resource access. Culture is treated as an operating system that constrains strategy; people, talent, and psychological safety are reframed as the assets worth protecting. A security-style playbook is revisited through awareness, asset visibility, incident learning, and data-driven measurement rather than headcount alone.

Closing guidance encourages practitioners to acknowledge personal blind spots, use privileged standing to support others, and invest resources so people feel safe enough to contribute. Audience questions extend the model to how under-representation weakens threat modeling and control choices, and how auditing and paired action can counter performative allyship.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2021-Christina Johns-Work SMTer Not Harder - Concolic Execution for CTF
talks.teaser: Shows how concolic execution with angr and Z3 can solve reverse engineering CTF challenges faster than manual analysis.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that automation helps with reverse engineering CTF challenges when there are many binaries or heavy computation. It introduces concolic execution, which mixes symbolic and concrete execution to find which inputs reach a target state. The speaker covers angr, a Python binary analysis framework, and Z3, an SMT solver that returns satisfying values for constraints or reports that none exist, and notes that it may not finish in reasonable time.

Three challenges show the approach. A challenge from the previous year's Diana CTF is solved with angr's find and avoid exploration, using the known flag length, printable-character constraints and the addresses of the win and fail prints. A redpwn 2020 challenge with around 5,000 comparisons maps well to direct Z3 constraints, though angr hooks for two slow library calls were another option. For FLARE 2018 Magic, shellcode for one algorithm is extracted, angr solves the first key piece from a blank state using a function that checks the return value, and the remaining keys follow by reimplementing the scrambling.

The closing points cover limits such as path explosion from loops and recursion, and library models that return symbolic values, so analysts should add the constraints they know about a program. Resources include angr's documentation, the angr CTF exercises and a Ghidra plugin for angr. In the Q&A the speaker explains exit criteria for extracted shellcode and notes that SMT solvers serve software verification and simplifying obfuscated malware.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2021-Kirsten Renner-TURNING BAD JOB ADS INTO OPPORTUNITIES!
talks.teaser: Participants learn to treat weak job postings as research prompts and advocate through recruiters and interviews.
talks.summary:
The session opens from a recruiting veteran’s view that most security job ads discourage strong candidates, especially people who hesitate when they do not match every line. Rather than waiting for employers to fix listings, the speaker frames each posting as a requirements exercise: infer what the company is really hiring for, then investigate whether that path fits your own needs and deal breakers.

The middle walks through LinkedIn research—other roles the company advertises, and employees already doing the target job—to see realistic career progression and whether credentials are truly mandatory. Buzzwords and bloated qualification lists are questioned instead of accepted; some ads target a unique individual, but parallel achievements may still justify a conversation. Recruiters are treated as partners when they represent the hiring company, and candidates are urged to raise mismatches early rather than silently disqualifying themselves.

The close stresses networking opportunities at virtual and hybrid events, using mock interviews to learn by questioning hiring managers, and applying anyway while clarifying red-flag language. The practical takeaway is that a bad ad can still launch disciplined company research, targeted questions, and interview advocacy aligned with your journey.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2021-Cassandra Brunetto-Vulnerabilities from Venus, Management from Mars: How to...
talks.teaser: Walks through how to scope and prioritise a new security program, from mapping crown jewels to setting realistic goals.
talks.summary:
The talk addresses someone newly hired to run a company's information security program who must build a strategy without becoming overwhelmed. It opens with breach cases: Yahoo's 2013 breach of three billion accounts, which drew an $85 million fine; Home Depot's 2014 compromise through stolen third-party credentials, followed by a $200 million fine; and Equifax's 2017 exposure of 150 million records, tied to an unpatched database framework and poor segmentation, which cost $575 million.

The first phase is discovery before any roadmap. The speaker recommends asking senior management and employees what the business does, what data it handles, and which regulations apply. Next come data classification, identifying the crown jewels and their owners, mapping where they live and who can reach them, and inventorying infrastructure and third-party vendors. Key players such as risk owners and subject-matter experts should be identified and cultivated, since they hold knowledge that outsiders miss. To define scope, compare the current state with the desired state using NIST implementation tiers, then apply threat modelling and risk assessment and prioritise the most serious risks.

For goals, the speaker advises SMART targets that align with the organisation's mission, and focusing on one area with significant gaps rather than many. Overcommitting leads to burnout, so project plans, realistic timelines, and outside consultants for short-term work help. Progress should be documented and reported, and small wins celebrated. In the Q&A, the speaker said few organisations have mapped their crown jewels, that small businesses need cost-benefit evidence, and that an asset inventory once turned up Windows XP systems with default admin privileges.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2021-Tanya Janca-Building Security Champions
talks.teaser: Explains how to recruit, train, reward and sustain security champions who extend an AppSec team's reach into developer teams.
talks.summary:
Tanya Janca argues that security teams cannot grow simply by working harder, and that a security champions program can extend their reach into development teams. She opens with the staffing gap, citing a figure she attributes to GitHub of roughly 500 software developers for each security person, and notes that hiring application security staff is hard. Her answer is a repeatable recipe: recruit, engage, teach, recognize, reward, and keep going.

On recruiting, she warns against assigning champions as punishment and wants managers on board first. Engagement means including champions in real incidents under need-to-know rules, sharing new policies and tools before anyone else, holding monthly check-ins, and staying calm when developers ask awkward questions. For teaching, she recommends limiting training to what developers will use, such as secure coding, threat modeling, relevant policies and the tools they run, rather than advanced network testing. Champions should not be handed work that belongs to AppSec, like giving security approvals, and should not validate static analysis results before they have training.

Recognition and reward were central for her: certificates, public shout-outs in team chat, notes in performance reviews, and emails to managers, plus low-cost rewards like baked goods, books or approved conference travel. She closes by warning that programs fade quickly, so teams should communicate regularly, even with a short email, and treat the program as an ongoing practice. The takeaway is that the program depends on trust, visible appreciation and consistency more than budget.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2021-Rin Oliver-Rising from the Ashes
talks.teaser: A keynote maps setbacks in pandemic-era job hunting to practical habits, community support, and boundaries for tech careers.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by describing a difficult path into information security and technology as a multiply neurodivergent person, including losing a long-held role after relocating from New Zealand to the United States and then facing pandemic layoffs, hurricanes in Louisiana, and a grueling search that yielded roughly two hundred applications, seven interviews, and many stalled or final-round rejections.

The middle of the talk turns those experiences into concrete recovery strategies: leaning on online vulnerability that led to a referral connection, side projects such as candle making to escape the rejection cycle, cheerleaders who advocate for hires, mentors with clear expectations, networking (especially low-pressure social events), learning paths that match how your brain works, hobbies and boundaries that resist grind culture, and professional help including therapy and mood tracking. The speaker argues resilience alone is insufficient without a nurturing community and warns that employers must set neurodivergent people up to win.

The closing message stresses that numerous rejections can precede a single affirmative answer, that marginalized candidates often face especially painful outcomes, and that setting boundaries protects worth at work and at home. A short Q&A covers therapist apps, preferring ghosting over lengthy rejections, and building neurodiversity employee resource groups with direct input from affected employees.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2021-@StephandSec-You Are the Prize: How to Hire the Right Boss & Employer for a...
talks.teaser: The session reframes job hunting so candidates interview employers and spot red flags before accepting offers.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by challenging how security professionals often approach hiring: anxious “pick me” thinking, survival-driven exits, and ambition that ignores culture and growth paths. A fictional practitioner named Sage illustrates imposter syndrome, bad boss fit, and repeating the same mistakes.

The core framework covers work done before applications—reflecting on what past roles provided or lacked, separating wants from needs, weighing mental health and life goals, and defining short- and long-term career direction. Interviews are reframed as mutual consultations. The speaker recommends prepared questions about daily workload, what colleagues love or dislike, advancement, and team structure, plus written non-negotiables and red flags such as vague answers, no training, rigid schedules, or solo-team overload. Mindset shifts treat the candidate as an asset with power to accept or decline.

After-interview reflection, self-reward, and refining criteria lead into networking paths (volunteering, speaking, meetups, social media) and a recommended career guide. Takeaways stress that you are your greatest asset, workplace quality shapes life outside work, self-worth counters imposter feelings, and leaving a bad manager is valid when the relationship cannot be fixed.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2021-Maker Village Day 1-Supernatural six build
talks.teaser: The session teaches hands-on through-hole soldering while assembling a fortune-display kit built around a Raspberry Pi Pico.
talks.summary:
The Maker Village host opens with sponsor thanks and a tour of bench gear: resistor benders, brass tip cleaners, side cutters, solder wick, solder suckers, ESD tweezers, magnifiers, and basic multimeter checks for resistance, diodes, and continuity. Attendees then build the Supernatural Six board step by step, starting with ten-ohm and sixty-eight-ohm resistors, then blue, green, and red LEDs located by flat sides and silkscreen marks.

Mid-session coverage includes fixing cold joints, excess solder, and filled holes using wick, reheating, table taps, or a vacuum desolder tool. Tactile buttons and a small OLED screen mount on the front; the screen shows humorous fortune text inspired by a classic magic-ball toy. On the back, female pin headers give a removable Raspberry Pi Pico, with male headers bridging into the socket before final soldering.

Practitioners leave with a finished through-hole kit, steady pin-header practice, and pointers toward a follow-on session for CircuitPython programming, USB power, optional portability, and blog documentation for working ahead.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2021-Suchismita Pahi -Leaders Lower the Ladder
talks.teaser: The session explores sponsorship, mentorship, outreach, and empathy as ways leaders widen access to cybersecurity careers.
talks.summary:
The presentation begins with U.S. cybersecurity diversity figures from 2019 and 2020, including women’s share of the workforce and senior management, and asks why capable community members are not reaching those roles. The speaker ties inclusion to product outcomes, describing tone-deaf marketing created without diverse input and early criticism of Snapchat’s automatic geolocation sharing, then to McKinsey-linked revenue statistics for ethnically and gender-diverse firms.

The “lower the ladder” framing contrasts ignoring, obstructing, or actively helping others climb. Operational advice separates sponsorship from general mentorship: sponsors promote work, navigate politics, assign visible stretch projects, and support promotion paths, while mentors advise over longer horizons inside or outside the organization. The talk covers making programs work through goals, feedback, peer exchange, and clear mentee expectations, plus outreach via accessible classes, guest lectures, school visits, donations to community groups, and talks to non-security professionals such as accountants on cyber insurance and regulations.

Closing emphasis falls on “aggressive empathy”—active listening, reflecting understanding, and aligning on feelings before solutions. Question-and-answer segments address practicing empathy without mirroring every emotion, winning over DEI skeptics through consistent ally example, mentoring from individual contributor roles via shared study time, being a coachable mentee, signaling openness as a leader, and relying on mentors for institutional history when driving change.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2021-Alyssa Miller-Sparking your security career: You can't get burned if you're...
talks.teaser: Explains how career fears, imposter syndrome and salary talks can hold security professionals back, and how to move past them.
talks.summary:
Alyssa Miller, a business information security officer at a credit ratings firm, opens by asking why capable people hold back from career moves. She traces her own path: a programming job at 19, a move into penetration testing at 28 after a manager asked her to join, and later consulting and leadership roles. Being passed over for a director role at 41 damaged her confidence, and an unexpected executive search later helped her see her record more clearly.

The middle of the talk covers barriers that hit some groups harder, including parental leave gaps and a lack of visible role models. Miller argues that imposter syndrome grows from comparing your narrow expertise with the apparent knowledge of others, and that skills from unrelated jobs still count in security. She calls job postings with long requirement lists unrealistic, advises applicants to focus on the core role, and recommends checking salary ranges on public sites and asking recruiters for pay bands. She also urges negotiating beyond base pay, such as bonuses or vacation time, and asking for feedback after a rejection.

She describes mentoring as more than skills coaching, built on trust and a personal connection, where mentors can become network allies. Her closing message is to treat setbacks as learning, recognise your own accomplishments, and help others grow. She illustrates the last point with thank-you notes from girls in a cybersecurity camp who were inspired by her story.

talks.title: TDI 2021 Speaker Wrangler walkthrough
talks.teaser: A practical walkthrough shows village MCs how to manage Hopin streams, moderators, sponsor slides, and audience engagement between talks.
talks.summary:
The session explains how village MC duties differ from main-stage hosting and walks through joining a village session on the virtual platform. The presenter opens a teen village room, enables microphone and camera after moderator approval, and shows how moderators approve or reject participants from the stream. They cite a GAO report that puts global facial recognition revenue at three to five billion dollars and projects growth toward ten billion, while noting that granted patents do not prove products are being built.

Law enforcement use gets close attention, including Amazon Ring partnerships with police departments, neighborhood video request services, and state arrangements for FBI photo searches. The speakers point to masked-face selfies that can feed training data, and to NIST testing that found masks raised false non-match rates for every one-to-one algorithm submitted before COVID-19. They also cover Clearview AI, which faces lawsuits and regulator inquiries and holds a 224 thousand dollar ICE contract, and NEC, which they say works with over a third of US state police agencies and with airport biometrics. A stadium scan of about 30,000 Rose Bowl attendees illustrates crowd surveillance.

Their takeaways are that large technology firms have stepped back from some facial recognition work while partners, foundations and side businesses continue it, and that the lack of federal privacy law leaves states such as Illinois, through its biometric privacy act, to drive class actions. Practitioners should push lawmakers, limit their own biometric exposure, and build with misuse in mind. The Q&A covered educating family members, posting photos of children, and what a biometric breach would mean.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2020 - Moving left in the SDLC
talks.teaser: Argues for bringing security checks earlier into each development phase, from design reviews to production testing.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why web application security is falling behind fast software delivery. Cloud services and continuous pipelines are cited as drivers, alongside figures: the Verizon 2020 DBIR linked web applications to more than 43 percent of breaches, and one survey found that 40 percent of retail applications were scanned only once a year. Penetration testing and a web application firewall are common, but they tend to surface problems after code is already live.

The core proposal is to move left in the software development lifecycle and bring security in from the design phase onward. In design, the speaker recommends reviewing data flow diagrams, classifying data, using current encryption algorithms, and checking whether internal APIs are exposed and vendors are assessed. In build, code scanning inside the CI/CD pipeline can catch issues such as hard-coded passwords, supported by developer training. In test and release, web applications and APIs are tested in a production-like environment for problems such as session management and cross-site scripting. After deployment, regular penetration tests continue.

The closing argument is that tooling alone is not enough. Teams need a security culture built with developers through competitions or hackathons, plus a dashboard tracking high-risk applications, open issues and fix times, with escalation for items left open too long.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2020 - Abhijith B R (abx) - Internal Red Team Operations Framework
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Diana Initiative 2020 - Abhijith B R (abx) - Internal Red Team Operations Framework - Building ....
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk presented at Diana Initiative 2020, Abhijith B R (known as abx) presents a structured methodology called the Internal Red Team Operations Framework (IRTOF). The framework is designed to help organizations transition from traditional internal penetration testing and vulnerability assessments toward a mature, practical internal red teaming program. The speaker emphasizes that while vulnerability assessments produce exhaustive lists of flaws and penetration tests focus on compromising specific targets, red teaming represents a full-scope adversarial simulation aimed at testing people, processes, and technology across the entire organization to systematically enhance defensive capabilities.

### Key Topics
- **Distinction Between Disciplines**: Clarifying the differences between vulnerability assessment (listing all potential weaknesses), penetration testing (goal-oriented compromise of specific targets), and red teaming (full-scope adversarial simulation aimed at challenging defensive measures).
- **The IRTOF Phased Progression**: A five-phase progressive roadmap modeled from "crawling" to "flying" (Phase 1: Crawling, Phase 2, Phase 3, Phase 4: Running, and Phase 5: Flying).
- **Team Composition and Skill Sets**: Building a multidisciplinary offensive unit inspired by diverse teams like The A-Team, including both deeply technical operators and non-technical advisors who can assist with realistic social engineering and business communications.
- **Collaboration with Blue Teams**: Emphasizing that red teams exist to make defenders stronger, advocating for continuous purple teaming and constructive relationships rather than adversarial friction.
- **Strategic vs. Tactical Execution**: Structuring the framework as individual short-term tactical plans (spanning 3 to 6 months per phase) chained together into an overarching long-term strategic plan.

### Technical Details
IRTOF breaks down red team maturity into five distinct phases:
1. **Phase 1 (Crawling / Foundation)**: Securing executive budget approval, establishing rules of engagement with legal and leadership oversight, defining clear objectives focused on protecting critical organizational crown jewels and sensitive data, identifying vulnerable key personnel, evaluating the existing security posture, and recruiting core talent.
2. **Phase 2 (Initial Operations & Emulation)**: Setting up external infrastructure (cloud environments, domain names, email hosting) and leveraging open-source command-and-control (C2) frameworks, implants, and tools. Initiating adversary emulation using open-source resources like MITRE ATT&CK, Atomic Red Team, and Caldera to test antivirus, EDR, and SOC logging. Mapping external attack surfaces, establishing remediation processes, and running basic phishing campaigns across employee tiers to test mail filters and proxy controls.
3. **Phase 3 (Improvisation & Process Maturation)**: Advancing tools, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) when standard methods are restricted (e.g., employing unmanaged PowerShell when standard PowerShell is blocked). Testing and attempting continuous EDR and antivirus bypasses, identifying exploitation paths toward crown jewels, evaluating incident response times and containment procedures, conducting automated emulation campaigns across random machines, and drafting formal operational documentation.
4. **Phase 4 (Running / Collaboration & Physical Assessment)**: Transitioning into continuous, collaborative purple team exercises and incorporating enterprise tooling alongside open-source platforms. Executing targeted spear-phishing campaigns against executives and management using custom tooling rather than easily detectable frameworks. Conducting overt physical security assessments (official walk-throughs inspecting doors, locks, RFID checkpoints, and CCTV, referencing work by Deviant Ollam) with proper operational security (avoiding tactical backpacks or sticker-covered laptops), and instituting continuous operator/defender training.
5. **Phase 5 (Flying / Full Maturity)**: Achieving advanced internal capabilities, including internally developed custom C2 platforms, custom implants, and exploit scripts. Running a formal purple team metrics model to evaluate blue team coverage and red team progress. Conducting covert physical security assessments once organizational trust and confidence are established, executing continuous adversary simulation, and running iterative cycles of the IRTOF operational process.

### Takeaways
Building an effective internal red team requires incremental growth rather than jumping immediately into complex, covert operations. By viewing each IRTOF phase as an achievable 3-to-6-month tactical plan, security leaders can progressively assemble diverse talent, establish open-source infrastructure, advance to custom development, and integrate collaborative purple team exercises that continually challenge and enhance the organization's overall cyber defense posture.

She is not a lawyer or therapist but worked with both, and stresses that harassment law has lagged behind online life while statutes in places such as Colorado and Arkansas still offer hooks for electronic bullying and threatening conduct. She clarifies that free speech does not cover intent to harm, and that cheap online lookups make physical stalking less necessary.

Practical lessons include engaging counsel before blocking so evidence is preserved, forwarding messages instead of replying, and staying factual in court rather than trading insults that become evidence against the victim. She used FMLA for trauma leave, secured a protective order, and routed new messages through her attorney. She cites Megan Meier Foundation work and youth cyberbullying statistics on reporting, self-harm, and suicide risk, and notes how always-on devices erase the old refuge of home.

She acknowledges missteps such as apologizing to the harasser and internalizing their narrative, including counselor work on Stockholm syndrome and reclaimed self-esteem. The session closes on recognizing withdrawal from games or phones, checking on others, taking recovery one second at a time, and the value of no reply when abuse continues unbidden.

The presenter traces a life moving through indigenous and American schooling, goth-era Linux startups, and a period of outsized career success after adopting confrontational leadership habits learned in a desert festival culture. As VP of engineering, they were asked to scale hiring using a name- and marker-blinded pipeline modeled on large Silicon Valley practice, and argues that bias still enters through résumé language, screeners, interviewers who see or hear candidates, and committees that never meet applicants.

Burnout, coming out as trans, and time away led to therapy, reflection on color perception as a literal bias metaphor, and a model of perception bias combining sensory input, bodily state, and memory. Meditation practice is framed as training to observe thoughts without letting them dictate reactions, with parallels to needing help when exercise hurts.

Re-entering tech brought repeated whiteboard-style panels, stereotype threat, awkward campus logistics, and pushback from numerous employers before one manager admitted not knowing how to hire someone like them; they eventually returned via a major vendor on open source work. The close ties these lessons to machine learning systems that encode historical injustice, urges crossing cultural comfort zones and valuing human biological diversity, and recommends meditation and honest panel dialogue as practical ways to notice bias without pretending it can be erased.

talks.summary:
The talk covers how abusers use everyday technology to watch, track and control a partner, and what someone leaving that situation can do about it. The speaker treats the problem as an information security task, but puts personal safety first: getting out of a dangerous situation comes before any data concern. Preparation for leaving includes a packed bag with identification, cash and a spare phone.

Much of the middle focuses on the accounts and devices a victim still shares with a former partner. Suggested steps include changing passwords and security questions on a clean machine, checking connected devices on the Wi-Fi router and phone, and turning off location sharing and family sharing. The speaker also points to message forwarding, cloud data exports, saved keychain passwords, and leftover devices and printers as ways data leaks out. Smart home gear, such as doorbells, cameras and voice assistants with shared access, can give an ex-partner live video, audio and control of alarms. Social media posts, fitness routes, delivery histories and shared calendars or travel itineraries can reveal a person's patterns.

The talk closes by stressing documentation: logging incidents as they happen, keeping an indexed record, and filing reports with police and the identity theft reporting site. Victims are urged to keep more than one backup of key evidence. The speaker's main message is that asking for help is the hardest step, and that documenting events and reporting them is what makes a case stick.
