talks.title: Diana Initiative 2020 - A case against “Google it”: A cognitive science approach
talks.teaser: Explains why sending newcomers to open web search harms learning and walks through cognitive apprenticeship for security mentoring.
talks.summary:
The speaker argues that telling a mentee to “just Google it” often worsens learning instead of fixing it. Unfiltered search results create information overload; many tutorials assume background the learner lacks; and newcomers frequently cannot form a useful query after dense training. He frames the problem with cognitive load theory—working memory limits, intrinsic and extraneous load, and what helps material reach long-term memory—and contrasts careless searching with deliberate questioning skills such as the question formula technique.

Using a fictional Windows system administrator with fifteen years of experience who wants to move into cybersecurity and learn Linux, he walks through cognitive apprenticeship phases. In modeling he maps familiar Windows ideas (profiles under Users, Active Directory, GUI permissions) to Linux tasks such as user creation, `/home`, shells versus Command Prompt, `chmod`, and optional Webmin for lower extraneous load. Scaffolding builds on that base with password policy via `login.defs`, vertical transfer (`netstat`, `ls` versus `dir`, routing), and harder horizontal transfer such as Samba file shares. Fading and coaching narrow problems (for example securing Apache or adding TLS to sendmail) while the mentor steps back and only reinforces fundamentals when the mentee is stuck.

Practitioners are urged to build trust first, use reflection and written explanations, teach advanced search operators and reputable sources instead of dumping URLs, reduce acronym load for beginners, and design boot camps and class time around metacognition. The arc ends with the mentee largely autonomous and able to help the mentor in return.

talks.teaser: Frames DevSecOps as a team sport, covering shared ownership, trust, communication and pacing for security-minded teams.
talks.summary:
The talk treats DevSecOps as a collective effort rather than a solo task, bringing development, security and operations teams together. It describes the friction that usually appears along the way, including turf wars, uneven skills, and security being seen as a final gate that says no. The main remedy offered is early, open communication, with security moved further left in the software lifecycle so it becomes a partner rather than an obstacle.

The middle of the talk covers how shared ownership and skills that can be swarmed to where demand rises help break down silos. Blameless failure is presented as a way for teams to learn quickly without fear. A grid of organisational archetypes is laid out, ranging from all-in and siloed teams to all-dev, fortress-style and well-oiled DevOps setups, each with different trade-offs between speed, trust and security. Measurement is also covered: value should be tied to business outcomes and tracked with both qualitative and quantitative measures, because return on investment fits many organisations poorly.

The closing advice is to pace the change, starting with a few smaller projects so the process becomes routine before scaling up. Leaders are urged to support their teams rather than pull them along. A parable about fishing for the village rather than relying on a single captain stresses that success depends on people working together and sharing both wins and lessons.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2020 - Carlota Sage, Don Donzal, Ping Look, Sara Pickering
talks.teaser: Panelists discuss hiring, resumes and career changes for people breaking into infosec from non-technical backgrounds.
talks.summary:
This career village panel from the virtual Diana Initiative 2020 addresses people moving into information security, many from non-IT backgrounds, amid widely reported talk of a skills shortage. Three panelists introduce their own paths: Ping Look, a senior director leading Microsoft's customer-facing detection and response team, began in graphic design and event work; Sara Pickering, a talent development director, started as an IT recruiter; Carlota Sage, a consultant, moved from web development and chemistry into security strategy.

The panelists explain hiring from three sides. Carlota favors people who fit the culture and learn quickly, especially at nonprofits that can invest in training. Sara notes that applicant tracking systems rely on keywords, so referrals, plain text-searchable resumes and a tailored base resume for each job description help candidates get seen. Ping looks for genuine motivation, varied experience and a systems-level view of security, and treats narrow focus and constant negativity as red flags. Thoughtful questions in interviews are stressed throughout.

The closing advice centers on honesty, since inflated skills tend to surface after hiring and damage trust. Listing CTFs, labs and personal projects on a resume, researching salary and company reviews before negotiating, and leaning on recruiters and personal networks are also recommended. Accepting an imperfect first role is framed as a learning step, provided the employer's values match yours.

talks.teaser: Explains what threat hunters do, which skills and tools they rely on, and how hunting supports incident response.

The talk introduces threat hunting and the people who do it, using the speaker's own casework as examples. One case involved tracking a malware group's use of macros and a downloader called Hancitor, where reviewing API calls revealed where code was hidden and how the payload was carved out of a running process. Another involved an intruder who repeatedly tried to upload a backdoor after a low-level alert, and a separate Coinhive alert that turned out to be browser-based cryptojacking rather than an infected host.

The speaker separates two common kinds of hunter. Those in SOC or incident response teams search endpoint and log data for missed indicators, and they often turn their findings into signatures and actionable advice after an incident. Researchers at security companies or government agencies hunt using open-source intelligence and track malware evolution, actor techniques and new CVEs. Skills covered include malware analysis, reverse engineering, attacker-mindset training and network analysis from packet captures, along with lists of tools for network, malware, link and dark web analysis. Scope, ticketing and shared notes are presented as ways to keep the work focused.

The closing argument is that organizations should understand the threats relevant to their own sector, since antivirus and endpoint products alone do not supply that intelligence. Hunters add a proactive view of adversaries and help move teams from reactive to proactive. The talk ends with learning resources and advice on building hands-on experience through CTFs and by recreating malware analysis in a home lab.

The talk opens by defining neurodiversity as an umbrella term that covers conditions such as autism, ADHD, Tourette's, dyspraxia, dyslexia and dyscalculia. The speaker argues that contributing to open source, often recommended as a way into a tech career, can be hard for neurodivergent people. Jargon, unclear contribution guidelines, long documentation and no clear person to ask questions all get in the way. Suggested fixes include accessible docs, defined contributor pathways and a named contact for questions, with a Kubernetes contributor experience group cited as an example.

The middle section turns to hiring and career progression. Culture-fit interviews, scripted behavioural questions and video screening were described as carrying bias against neurodivergent candidates. Performance improvement plans were said to penalise people for not meeting neurotypical output norms. For employers, the speaker recommended lower-visibility screening, setting performance goals together with the employee, and creating employee resource groups. Audience questions covered interview design, whether to disclose a disability on job applications, and where neurodivergent people can find learning resources. The speaker's answer was that community support tends to work better than self-study.

The closing part gave allies practical starting points, including autistic self-advocacy resources and opening a workplace dialogue without putting colleagues on the spot. The main takeaway was to talk with neurodivergent people rather than about them, and to ask them what success and inclusion look like.

Amanda Draeger opens by explaining that her talk is about textile crafts rather than the strings command-line tool. She traces punch cards back to Jacquard looms, points out that knitting and crochet patterns read a lot like machine code, and describes how months of sewing cloth masks during the pandemic showed her that the same principles apply across crafts and computing.

The middle of the talk works through several lessons. Understanding how a sewing machine loops its two threads lets you diagnose tension problems directly instead of looking up the manual each time. For automation, she suggests asking which step is physically painful, where human error is easiest, and whether the task will stay the same. Her bias tape jig suits a repeated, fixed-size job, but making different widths might not justify a new jig. Batch processing saved time until she over-batched mask pieces that tangled together, which cost more time than cutting between them would have. Weaving rewards planning with a draft, while crochet allows more improvisation, so the right amount of planning depends on whether a project is a quick fix or something meant to last. Tool choice follows the same logic: an electric spinner suits home use, while a simple hand spindle is better for carrying around.

She closes by arguing that every field has useful lessons and that people new to security often bring experience from other parts of the world. Taking time to learn from them, she says, is worth the effort.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2020 - 7 Tips for Women To Get To the Top in Technology
talks.teaser: Offers seven practical strategies for women in tech to advance their careers, from finding allies to demanding specific feedback.
talks.summary:
This pre-recorded session, presented for the Diana Initiative, is built around seven tips for women who want to reach senior roles in technology. The speaker, Perrine Farque, draws on about a decade of leading marketing strategy at software companies. She argues that the gender gap has widened since the pandemic pushed many women out of the workforce, and that diverse teams tend to produce more innovative products and stronger financial results, so women's advancement matters to businesses as well as to individuals.

The middle of the talk works through the tips in order. Find allies such as sponsors and champions who speak up for you when you are not in the room, and nurture those relationships. Say your career goals out loud, even if it risks seeming less likeable, and ask for stretch assignments. Request high-profile glamour work instead of office housework, and ask for wholehearted recommendations, since hedged wording can hurt a candidate's chances. Build a diverse network to widen opportunities beyond people who look and think like you. In meetings, rotate note-taking and admin tasks, redirect questions aimed at a male colleague when you are the most qualified person present, use amplification so that others repeat a woman's point, and steer off-topic challenges back to the agenda.

The final tip covers feedback. Citing Stanford research on performance reviews at three large tech companies, the speaker says women receive vaguer feedback than men, with praise centred on team contribution and criticism focused on personality rather than outcomes. She closes by urging listeners to be proactive, vocal and intentional about mentors and sponsors, and to ask for specific, outcome-based feedback. Viewers are invited to share their own top tip online.

talks.teaser: Explores overlooked MFA weaknesses and shows how second-factor logs expose sharing, shadow IT, and ongoing attacks.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by leveling the audience on how multi-factor authentication fits after primary login, then contrasts common vendor promises—password-policy relief and blocked credential reuse—with persistent attack paths such as push spam, man-in-the-middle phishing, admin bypass abuse, misconfigured applications that skip the second factor, red-team enrollment while users are away, and fail-open designs when the MFA service cannot be reached.

The core work is operational threat hunting in MFA telemetry. The speaker walks through log fields including access client, enrolled device, factor type, integration context, and source IP, stressing that location and device metadata need cross-checks against directory data, asset inventories, and internal DNS before they drive conclusions. Correlation with first-factor logs is presented as essential. Real-world vignettes illustrate multiple accounts tied to one shared desk phone with automatic tone acceptance, shadow IT logins through a colleague’s landline, benign duplicate device records after phone upgrades, contractor phones on a former employee’s account, typo-driven wrong-number pushes, and scripted five-minute-interval attempts against someone on leave.

Practical takeaways emphasize limiting self-enrollment, reconsidering phone-call factors, hardening bypass processes, educating users on reporting odd prompts and credential-sharing pressure, and treating MFA as something to monitor and tune—not deploy once and ignore.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2020 - So, I Made A Microdot
talks.teaser: Walks through the history of microdots and shows how one is made with a film camera and a kitchen counter.
talks.summary:
Emily Crose opens with the history of the microdot, a document photographed and shrunk to a speck. The technique dates to the late 1800s, was used to carry messages by homing pigeon in World War One, and later appeared in Cold War espionage and in personal keepsakes. The talk explains that the small size, and the need for a lens or microscope to read it, made the format useful for covert transfer.

The middle of the talk covers production in two stages. In the first, a document is photographed with a 35 millimeter camera on high-grain black and white film, with the page filling the viewfinder, and the negative is cut to frame. Moving the camera farther from the page gives a macro dot of about 1.5 centimeters that can be read by eye when backlit. In the second stage, a small section of that negative is cut out, backlit, and photographed again, producing a microdot about three millimeters long. The speaker's own attempt at this size was not readable without magnification, and she explained that focus, film contrast and focal length limit how small the result can get.

The talk ends with modern uses and ways to improve the result, such as using microfiche or higher-contrast film. Ideas discussed include storing a bitcoin key or one-time pads, and hiding data in ultra high resolution images. The main takeaway is that the method needs little specialized equipment, but it is labor-intensive, hard to handle, and relies on obscurity rather than encryption.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2020 - TechGirlMN - Workshop 2 of 5 - “Off the Shelf” Breadboard addition
talks.teaser: Guides attendees through Arduino Nano breadboard wiring for seven LEDs, resistors, jumpers, a push button, and IDE upload tests.
talks.summary:
The session opens with solderless breadboard mechanics and mounting an Arduino Nano so both pin rows remain usable. Participants insert seven 220-ohm resistors on the negative rail, place large 10mm LEDs with short cathode legs through the resistors, and leave the long anode legs free for jumpers while the presenter shares spacing and optional leg-trimming tips.

Wiring continues with rail bridges, color-coded jumpers from each LED anode to digital outputs (documented as D2–D8, with a later scope check showing a one-pin shift on the demo board), plus power and ground ties to the Nano’s 5V and GND. A capped push button on D10 uses a pull-up and orange jumpers, including routing through a spare column when jumper lengths fall short.

The latter portion moves to the Arduino IDE: choosing Nano/328p boards, trying old versus new bootloaders on clones, and editing the Blink sketch with a define to drive external pins instead of the built-in LED. A faulty demo board forces live troubleshooting, while working uploads show pin-by-pin blinking, linked grab-and-go ASCII patterns, and a stock button sketch that lights an LED on press. The presenter assigns verifying all seven LEDs as follow-up work and previews upcoming coding, Tinkercad, and soldering sessions in the five-part series.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2020 - TechGirlMN - Workshop 4 of 5 - Basic Arduino coding using virtual Badge
talks.teaser: A virtual badge workshop walks through C-style Arduino code that chases LEDs across pins and flips direction when a button is pressed.
talks.summary:
The session is the fourth in a series on a Diana Initiative virtual conference badge. Participants who cloned the public Tinkercad project move from block logic to hand-written sketch code on a simulated breadboard, using the same badge design introduced the day before.

The instructor walks through void setup (pin modes for a button on pin 10 and LED outputs on pins 2 through 9, plus Serial.begin at 9600) and void loop conventions in a C-like dialect: digitalRead, digitalWrite, delay in milliseconds, global variables such as active_led and active_led2, and Serial.println for tracing. Starting from a press-to-light example, the sketch lights LEDs in sequence, increments the active pin, resets when active_led reaches 9 or above, then adds button state so the forward chase runs in one branch and an else branch decrements toward pin 8 with a lower bound of 1. Live edits fix syntax errors, clarify bounds checking, sync active_led2 when the button toggles direction, and correct copy-paste variable names.

The presenter plans to publish the finished sketch on a personal site and link an online Arduino editor project, with optional code for a physical board. A chat reference notes an alternate Larson-scanner style implementation adapted from another contributor’s repository. The hour ends with contact details and encouragement to experiment further.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2020 - Career Village
talks.teaser: A security recruiter shares resume tips on layout, section order, length and matching LinkedIn profile advice.
talks.summary:
The talk is a set of resume tips from Chrissy Morgan, who works at a security staffing agency and volunteers in the Career Village. She begins with the advice to keep one general master resume and copy it into tailored versions for each job. She notes that recruiters spend only seconds on a first scan, so name, contact details and key skills should sit near the top, with experience in reverse-chronological order and full month and year dates.

The middle covers layout and content. Education and certifications go lower, followed by community involvement such as meetings, talks, papers, bootcamp teaching, bug bounty work or a public GitHub profile. She argues that a security resume can run to two or three pages, and that a one-page limit is a myth. Formatting should use one typeface and three to seven bullets per job, with the wording rewritten rather than pasted from a posting. Spelling and grammar errors and unexplained employment gaps are flagged as things that hurt a first impression.

The closing section moves to LinkedIn. She recommends matching the profile to the resume, including consistent dates, a recent professional photo and a headline listing specific skills, since recruiters search by keyword. The talk ends with her contact details and a pointer to another Career Village talk on interview advice.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2020 - Career Village
talks.teaser: Guidance for hiring managers on lean interview panels, interview quality, and fast structured feedback to reduce candidate drop-off.
talks.summary:
The presentation targets hiring managers who want to shrink bottlenecks when filling security roles. It builds on an earlier installment and opens with the idea that slow, low-quality hiring timelines push strong applicants toward other employers, multiply competing offers, and delay decisions until preferred candidates are gone. The speaker structures the rest around three areas: who sits on the interview panel, how those conversations run, and how feedback is collected and relayed.

Interview panels should stay as small as practical. Larger groups rarely improve retention yet make unanimous support harder, which can yield prolonged searches, no hire at all, or new hires without full team backing. Each participant needs a clear slice of the job description to assess, and the full panel should meet beforehand so roles, order, and expectations align. Sequencing matters so deal-breakers surface early rather than after many wasted rounds. Hiring managers are urged to observe how colleagues actually interview, catching duplicated questions, scope creep, and questions that create legal or HR risk.

Feedback should be captured immediately after each session, with enough detail that recruiters are not guessing days later or confusing candidates. Positive outcomes deserve the same speed and depth as rejections, because delayed responses signal disinterest in a tight talent market. The closing reminder ties reputation effects in a small industry back to the same theme: lengthy, unfocused processes cost more than time alone.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2020 - Career Village
talks.teaser: Explains how to make job offers candidates accept, covering expectations, competitive terms and response deadlines.
talks.summary:
Chris from Tyro Security closes a short video series, made with the Diana Initiative, on fixing common problems in the hiring process. This final part focuses on the offer stage. He argues that a hiring team should learn what a candidate needs well before making an offer, and that expectations shift over a long process, so they should be checked again rather than assumed.

He then covers how to make the offer easy to accept. Rather than trimming terms, he suggests trying to beat what the candidate expects, such as a higher salary, a sign-on bonus or extra stock, where the budget allows. He also stresses a realistic deadline. In his experience, candidates who have been engaged throughout usually decide within a couple of days. A long silence, or a candidate taking the full length of a generous window, may mean they are weighing another offer, using it to negotiate with a current employer, or buying time for another interview.

The closing message is that the offer stage rests on everything done earlier in the process. Showing candidates that they are valued makes the final close far easier, while skipped steps leave the employer unsure whether they will get the person.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2020 - Career Village
talks.teaser: Practical guidance on writing simple and expanded security job descriptions that widen the candidate pool and support diversity.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens on a recurring hiring failure: weak job descriptions that shrink the applicant pool, lower candidate quality, and make it harder to interview people from underrepresented backgrounds in cybersecurity. The speaker frames this as the first installment in a partnership series focused on where recruiting processes break down.

The core advice is to maintain two versions of every role posting. A short external-facing description should list only true essentials and clear job tasks, kept to roughly five broad competencies rather than certifications or learnable tools unless a skill is non-negotiable for short-term success. A richer internal or late-stage description reuses those essentials, adds desirables for medium- and long-term growth, repeats tasks, and may name tools so candidates understand the environment—while warning that HR or recruiters may misuse tool lists as keyword filters.

The talk closes by urging simplicity throughout the hiring pipeline, noting that investing in medium-term skills aids retention, and pointing listeners to LinkedIn for follow-up questions as the series continues.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2020 - Hopin Backstage Admin How to handle a Recorded Talk
talks.teaser: Shows Hopin backstage admins how to run a recorded YouTube talk, switch sources, and handle audience refresh delays.
talks.summary:
The session targets backstage administrators who must put pre-recorded talks on a Hopin stage instead of a live presenter. It walks through staying on the correct stage in the admin view, approving and broadcasting a speaker wrangler for introductions and sponsor messaging, and keeping both the backstage view and the event dashboard open while working in edit mode.

The core workflow is switching the stream provider from Hopin to a saved YouTube link, stopping broadcast, and using force reset so attendees see the video. Repeated demos highlight operational pain points: roughly a ten-second delay can air unwanted footage, the stage can show stream disconnected until viewers hard refresh, and the interface may read as live while output is still YouTube.

Practitioners should plan dry runs on a test instance, arrive early on show day, and rely on moderators to prompt forced browser refreshes when flipping from live to recorded content. Running two monitoring setups is recommended because the platform gives limited feedback during source changes.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2020 - Hopin virtual venue overview for attendees 1
talks.teaser: A Hopin walkthrough orients attendees to reception resources, talk stages, villages, networking, expo booths, and safety reporting.
talks.summary:
The presentation orients Diana Initiative attendees to the year’s Hopin-based virtual venue before the live event begins. Viewers learn how ticket holders use their Hopin link to enter the event or preview mode, and how the reception area centralizes policies, schedules, FAQs, sponsor swag, merchandise, and paths to the information booth or safety operations room when problems arise.

The middle of the walkthrough covers main stage talk tracks with stage-level and event-wide chat, polls, attendee lists, and direct messages with optional video calls or muting. Separate sessions host the career village, capture the flag room, information booth, and scheduled badge workshops, including when sharing audio and video requests presenter status. Attendees can add moderated community sessions, with guidance on participant limits for on-camera slots, recording costs, the networking roulette area, and post-talk social hours.

Practitioners attending the conference should treat this as a logistics map: know where talks versus villages live, use moderated rooms when hosting discussions, avoid accidental unmoderated sessions, and plan time for expo booths and sponsored giveaways alongside the formal schedule.
